Abstract
AI incident reporting requirements are emerging in regulation and policy, yet no operational criteria
exist for determining when a detected AI incident warrants escalation beyond national handling to
international coordination. This paper proposes an escalation framework to address this gap, intended
as a common reference point across jurisdictions that enables aligned escalation while preserving
flexibility in how actors respond within their own legal and policy contexts. Our methodology
involves a review of SB 53, the EU AI Act, the GPAI Code of Practice, and incident frameworks
from other industries, to derive eight criteria to assess whether an incident warrants escalation, which
we then translate into a sequential flowchart with gated decision points and threshold checks. For
each criterion, we map how it interplays with the EU AI Act, SB 53, and the GPAI Code of Practice,
identifying where these frameworks’ design choices support or undermine effective detection. We
test the framework against ten documented AI incidents and structured variants to identify where
escalation criteria under-detect or misclassify incidents in practice. We find three design patterns that
may lead to systematic under-detection or misclassification of AI incidents in regimes where model
developers are responsible for escalation: (a) where escalation requires confirmed harm, events such as
model weight exfiltration or credible CBRN threats risk detection only after severe, irreversible harm
has propagated, as developers who observe the risk materializing cannot confirm downstream harms;
(b) where incidents are assessed only individually, systemic harms emerging from accumulation —
such as large-scale manipulation and psychological harm — risk being under-detected; and (c) where
thresholds align with legal instruments rather than quantitatively testable terms, criteria risk being
impractical to apply under time pressure. We also find that escalation rules are only one component
of a broader framework: the underlying definitions against which thresholds are set, and the data
available to the responsible actor, create interdependencies that can themselves drive under-detection
and must be addressed in framework design.

Executive Summary
As AI systems become more capable and are increasingly deployed across borders and sectors, incidents involving
these systems increasingly have international implications. Effective responses often depend on timely coordination
between governments, companies, and other stakeholders. However, existing approaches to incident reporting and
escalation vary widely, creating gaps in how risks are identified, assessed, and shared across jurisdictions.
A central question is when an AI incident should trigger an international response. For escalation to be effective
in practice, it must occur early enough to enable the benefits of cross-border coordination, such as containment,
mitigation, and shared response. This requires escalation thresholds and triggers that function reliably under real-world
conditions, both for novel forms of AI risk and across key domains of systemic AI risk, namely, large-scale manipulation
and psychological harm; loss of control; chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) threats; and cyber
vulnerabilities and offensive capabilities.
This paper presents an AI incident escalation framework intended to serve as a common reference point across
jurisdictions, enabling a more aligned approach to escalation while allowing flexibility in how actors respond within
their own legal and policy contexts. Our methodology involves a review of SB 53, the EU AI Act, the GPAI Code of
Practice, and incident frameworks from other industries, to derive eight criteria to assess whether an incident warrants
escalation, which we then translated into a sequential flowchart with gated decision points and threshold checks. We
test the framework against ten documented AI incidents and structured variants to identify where escalation criteria
under-detect or misclassify incidents in practice.
Incidents assessed using the framework are classified into one of three outcomes: escalation to trigger international
mobilization, an alert to provide capacity support or information, or no action, where an international response is not
warranted. To determine the outcome, the criteria first check whether the incident is in scope and if it represents a threat
triggering immediate escalation, otherwise they check for harm severity. Where current harm does not exceed severity
thresholds, criteria review the propagation path of the incident, to identify cross-border implications, and finally identify
potential residual irreversible harm with cross-border impacts.
Escalation rules are only one component of the broader escalation framework. Equally essential are the underlying
definitions against which thresholds and triggers are set, including incident types, risk pathways, harm categories,
severity scales, and clustering rules, and the data available to the actor responsible for determining whether a trigger
condition has been met.
• Definition gaps primarily affect domains where risk pathways and harm impacts are less mature: large-scale
manipulation, psychological harm, and loss-of-control risks. Specifically, we find harm severity scales lack adequate
categories for manipulation and psychological harm; and while regulators and developers have identified vulnerable
groups, notably children, as requiring heightened protection, no practical mechanism, such as vulnerability
modifiers, yet exists for adjusting severity assessments for incidents affecting these populations.
• Data gaps concern the dispersal of information needed to operate triggers across disconnected sources. The stress
testing revealed two qualitatively distinct problems. Cross-developer data: pattern-based triggers (cumulative
harms, shared failure modes, frequency acceleration) require visibility across providers, feasible only with shared
definitions, interoperable schemas, and data-sharing agreements. Cross-domain intelligence: state-orchestrated
incident clusters like the GRU-linked Pravda/Doppelgänger campaign produced no signal in any developer’s
systems and were detected only through national intelligence, investigative journalism, and media auditing,
requiring pre-specified interfaces with institutions whose mandates already cover adversarial campaign detection.
Escalation rules comprise the design of triggers and thresholds that determine the outcome for an assessed incident.
We identify three design patterns that may lead to systematic under-detection or misclassification of AI incidents.

While we group our findings by these categories, we also note that the interdependencies between them can themselves
be the underlying cause of particular findings. For example, we expect escalation rules for incidents relating to
manipulation and psychological harm are largely absent from escalation rules because the bounds of incidents and their
risk pathways in this domain have not be defined, severity scales are underdeveloped, and it is unclear which data would
needed to trigger these, and if this is available.
The proposed escalation framework and the identified design patterns are intended to support policymakers and
other relevant stakeholders worldwide who are developing or implementing AI incident reporting regimes. Emerging
approaches such as the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice and California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial
Intelligence Act (SB 53) illustrate the growing emphasis on reporting serious or critical AI incidents. This work aims to
inform such efforts by showing how the design and operationalization of escalation criteria can shape which incidents
are identified and escalated in practice, particularly under real-world constraints and across common risk pathways.

Introduction
The combination of more advanced capabilities, wider adoption, and increased affordances granted to AI systems
increases the likelihood of incidents occurring, but not all incidents represent the same potential for harm. Distinguishing
between incidents of differing severity is therefore critical for determining when and how to respond.
Yet even the foundational concept of an "AI incident" lacks a settled, operationally consistent definition. The OECD’s
stocktaking exercise on AI incident terminology found that existing definitions vary significantly across regulatory
instruments, incident databases, and the academic literature, differing on questions such as whether an AI system must
be the proximate cause of harm or merely a contributing factor, whether near-misses and hazards fall within scope,
and whether the definition requires actual harm or also covers credible risk of harm (OECD, 2023). The subsequent
OECD definitional paper proposed distinguishing between an AI incident, an event where the development, use, or
malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to actual harm; and an AI hazard, an event that could plausibly
lead to such an incident (OECD, 2024b). The AI Incident Database (AIID), the largest public repository of AI incidents,
adopts a broader formulation that includes alleged harms and near-harms (McGregor, 2021), and has itself evolved to
accommodate "issues", unrealized risks that do not meet incident ingestion criteria but advance understanding of where
AI presents the potential for harm (McGregor et al., 2022b). The EU AI Act takes a different approach, defining "a
serious incident" as one that directly or indirectly leads to death, serious health harm, irreversible disruption of critical
infrastructure, or fundamental rights violations (Art. 3(49)), while SB 53 introduces the distinct category of critical
safety incident” under a separate threshold.
Meanwhile, analytical work on failure taxonomies demonstrates that even when a definition is agreed, the causes and
boundaries of incidents remain subject to significant epistemic uncertainty, as the exact causes of AI incidents are
seldom fully known from public reporting alone (Pittaras and McGregor, 2023; Paeth et al., 2024b). This definitional
instability is not merely a taxonomic concern. The definition of an AI incident sets the boundary condition for every
downstream function: reporting obligations, threshold triggers, severity classification, and escalation criteria all inherit
the scope and limitations of the incident definition they are built on (OECD, 2024b). A definition that is too narrow
risks excluding incidents where AI played a material but non-proximate role; one that is too broad risks overwhelming
reporting and response systems with events that do not warrant coordinated action. Getting this formulation right has
been a persistent challenge for the AI incidents field, and it directly shapes the practical effectiveness of the escalation
framework we propose in this paper.
Scales have been proposed to distinguish between incidents of differing severity. The Future Society distinguishes
between an AI incident, which is limited in scope, contained without widespread spillover, and recoverable; an AI
emergency, a faster-moving, more urgent threat requiring immediate national or even international intervention; and an
AI crisis, the most severe stage of escalation, which is a disruption that causes large-scale harm, often spreading across
borders or sectors (Nguyen, 2025). AI crisis preparedness is defined as the capacity to prevent AI hazards, incidents,
and emergencies from escalating into a crisis, and to limit their impact if they do occur (Nguyen, 2025). Achieving
this requires enabling the early detection of AI hazards and incidents and responding to these appropriately across
jurisdictions and sectors.
The detection of AI incidents meeting certain severity thresholds is also addressed in regulation. The EU General-
Purpose AI Code of Practice (Commitment 9) requires signatories to report ‘Serious incidents’ to the EU AI Office
(Article 55(1)) and SB 53 (Labor Code §1107) introduces reporting requirements for ‘Critical safety incidents’ (European
Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024; European Commission, 2025; California State Legislature,
2025a). The definitions, thresholds, and escalation criteria within these serve as the mechanism for setting the criteria an
incident must meet to fall within their scope: defined correctly, these escalate all incidents warranting attention; flawed
design may lead to material incidents being missed, or low-severity incidents being captured. Furthermore, to isolate
the intended incidents in practice, escalation thresholds and triggers must function reliably under real-world conditions,
including time pressure, taking into account data access constraints and potential uncertainty around understanding
incidents as they are developing.
In this paper we focus on developing a framework to identify incidents that warrant international coordination. While
many open questions need to be addressed to design and operationalize a model for AI crisis preparedness, including
defining institutional responsibilities and the policy instruments that would govern it, this paper focuses on how a
detected incident can be evaluated against a set of eight criteria and thresholds to determine whether it warrants
international escalation. We address two questions:
1. What criteria, thresholds, and triggers should exist to determine whether an AI incident requires international
escalation?

2. How do the design choices of AI incident escalation criteria impact their effectiveness at detecting AI incidents
in practice?
To address these questions, we develop an AI incident escalation framework, designed as a sequential flowchart with
gated decision points and threshold checks, built around eight criteria for determining when an AI incident should be
escalated internationally. For each criterion, we map how it interplays with the EU AI Act, SB 53, and the GPAI Code
of Practice, identifying where these frameworks’ design choices support or undermine effective detection (European
Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024; European Commission, 2025; California State Legislature,
2025a). We test the framework against ten documented AI incidents and structured variants to identify where escalation
criteria under-detect or misclassify incidents in practice.
The regulatory analysis focuses on the EU AI Act (Arts. 3(49), 51, 73) and California’s SB 53 as the two most
developed legislative instruments that define incident escalation obligations for general-purpose AI, supplemented
by the GPAI Code of Practice as the principal means of operationalizing the EU regime (European Parliament and
Council of the European Union, 2024; European Commission, 2025; California State Legislature, 2025a). Cross-domain
design precedents are drawn from established escalation frameworks in nuclear safety, aviation, public health, financial
stability, cybersecurity, and disaster risk reduction. The framework and its thresholds are anchored to the state of these
instruments as of April 2026; as AI incident reporting regimes mature and new regulatory requirements emerge, the
escalation criteria will require reassessment against updated legal baselines.

Methodology
To develop threshold logic for classifying AI incidents that may warrant international coordination, we use a three-stage
sequential design in which each stage produces traceable inputs to the next, creating a path from reviewed literature to
final design choices. The following sections of the paper reflect these stages.
Stage 1: Literature review and requirement extraction.
The first stage draws on three bodies of literature:
how severe incidents are classified and escalated in established high-stakes domains (public health, nuclear safety,
cybersecurity, financial stability, and disaster risk reduction); current practical approaches and limitations in AI incident
monitoring; and AI incident escalation requirements in existing regulation, specifically the EU AI Act (Arts. 3(49), 51,
73) and California’s SB 53. These sources are used to characterize the structural dimensions along which incidents
vary and to identify which dimensions have operationalized scoring criteria adaptable to AI contexts. From this review,
common criteria for incident evaluation are identified and criteria selected for inclusion based on their relevance to the
escalation decision, the design precedent in established or emerging frameworks, and their operational feasibility under
realistic information constraints (Appendix C).
Stage 2: Threshold and indicator framework design.
The second stage translates the selected criteria into threshold
logic to define which questions need to be asked to evaluate an incident’s materiality for potential international escalation
(Appendix A). Eight assessment criteria are derived through a constrained design process. The objective is to identify
the minimum operational set of decision-relevant dimensions required to determine whether an incident warrants
international escalation and to provide a testable basis for the scenario-based stress testing. The criteria are combined
into a sequential flowchart logic with supporting threshold checks at each decision point. Criteria and threshold values
are defined separately: criteria specify what must be assessed, while threshold values are intentionally kept variable to
allow different risk tolerances to be applied. The intention is to make the framework adaptable to different escalation
rules without requiring changes to the underlying logic. For each criterion, we map how it interplays with the EU
AI Act, SB 53, the GPAI Code of Practice, and the key frameworks from other industries, identifying where these
frameworks’ design choices support or undermine effective detection.
As part of the framework design, we define the response classifications in Table 1 for criteria identified as relevant to
escalating an incident to the international level.
Stage 3: Scenario-based stress testing.

3
Literature review
3.1
AI incidents and the case for international escalation
To understand when AI incidents may warrant international escalation, it is useful to first consider how other domains
have approached cross-border incident response, before turning to emerging AI frameworks.
International frameworks for incident response are coordination mechanisms, including shared definitions, reporting
protocols, and cross-border response procedures that enable jurisdictions, developers, and affected parties to detect,
investigate, contain, and learn from incidents whose causes, effects, or remediation pathways span national boundaries.
They have evolved in domains where threats can cross borders because the systems through which they propagate are
themselves interconnected: pathogens travel through global mobility networks, cyberattacks through shared digital
infrastructure, and financial contagion through interlinked markets. Frameworks such as the World Health Organization’s
International Health Regulations (World Health Organization, 2005), the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime (Council
of Europe, 2001), and the Financial Stability Board’s coordination mechanisms (Financial Stability Board, 2012) were
established on the basis that delayed or siloed responses risk converting containable incidents into systemic crises.
Article 2 in the IHR articulates its purpose as preventing, protecting against, and controlling the international spread
of disease ‘in ways that are commensurate with and restricted to public health risks, and which avoid unnecessary
interference with international traffic and trade’ (World Health Organization, 2005). Defining such objectives explicitly
is what enables the success of an escalation framework to be measured against them.
Regulatory approaches to AI similarly define high-level objectives, though typically at the level of the overall regime
rather than incident escalation specifically. The EU AI Act’s stated purpose, per Article 1(1), is ‘to improve the
functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence
(AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including
democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union and
supporting innovation’ (European Parliament and Council, 2024). California’s SB 53, the Transparency in Frontier
Artificial Intelligence Act, addresses catastrophic risks from frontier foundation models through mandatory transparency,
incident reporting, and whistleblower protections (California State Legislature, 2025b).
Drawing on these defined objectives, we define the purpose of our AI international incident escalation framework as
enabling international action only where a purely national response is insufficient, and where harm, response capacity,
or control over the propagation pathway is distributed across jurisdictions. We identify three reasons why an AI incident
may require international escalation:
10


1. Cross-border harm. Harm has already been realized in multiple jurisdictions, necessitating coordination
across them. This represents the most direct trigger for international response, analogous to the WHO IHR’s
core criterion of ‘international spread of disease’ (World Health Organization, 2005) and the NIS2 criterion
for incidents affecting two or more Member States through shared infrastructure (European Parliament and
Council, 2022). Where harm is already distributed across jurisdictions, no single national authority possesses
sufficient observability or controllability to mount an adequate response independently.
2. Cross-border containment. There is a credible pathway for harm to spread that requires intervention outside
the originating jurisdiction. The incident may be localized at present but is actively propagating, with a
pathway that runs through infrastructure, models, or deployment patterns that cross borders. Containment
may require action in the jurisdiction where the upstream source sits or through which the pathway runs.
For example, this may arise in a deepfake political disinformation campaign. This mirrors the public health
rationale whereby containing an outbreak may require preventive measures at ports of entry in countries not
yet affected, and the cybersecurity principle that remediating a vulnerability requires cooperation from the
jurisdiction hosting the compromised infrastructure.
3. Irreversible harm within one jurisdiction with cross-border consequences. Harm may be contained and
not actively propagating, but permanent damage in one jurisdiction may generate downstream consequences
for others. Illustrative examples include a permanently corrupted financial dataset in one country’s market
infrastructure upon which other countries’ systems depend, or irreversible environmental harm that crosses
borders by nature.
We identify further conditions under which international action would be beneficial, but which are better characterized
as triggers for alert rather than escalation. These draw on frameworks whose primary purpose is the sharing of
learnings and mutual assistance rather than active containment, most notably civil aviation, where ICAO Annex 13
establishes a learning-first, non-punitive regime explicitly separated from liability and blame (International Civil
Aviation Organization, 2024). Whether an incident meets these conditions can be determined through the standard
incident assessment process, though in practice the resulting actions may be handled by coordination structures distinct
from those convened for escalation. These share the characteristic that international mobilization provides capacity or
information that would not otherwise be available:
1. Response capacity gap, where the affected jurisdiction lacks sufficient resources or information to respond
effectively, arising from the technical complexity of investigating frontier model behavior, the resource
demands of large-scale containment, or the absence of domestic expertise in the relevant AI capability domain.
2. Information gap, arising where understanding the incident requires data held across multiple jurisdictions,
such that no single actor possesses the complete picture necessary for effective response.
3. Enforcement capacity gap, where the affected jurisdiction lacks the legal authority, technical means, or
institutional reach to compel remediation from a developer headquartered elsewhere, arising from limits on
extraterritorial jurisdiction, gaps in mutual legal assistance frameworks for AI-specific harms, or the absence
of enforceable cross-border obligations on frontier developers.
4. Cross-developer control improvements, to notify model developers that controls which failed in one system
may be insufficient in analogous systems elsewhere, enabling preventive remediation across the sector before
similar failures materialize.
3.2
Requirements for escalation of AI incidents in regulation
Current regulation contains several drivers for AI incident escalation. This paper focuses on the EU AI Act, which
includes provisions relating to the escalation of ‘serious incidents’ and ‘prohibited practices’, and California’s Senate
Bill 53 (SB 53), which captures ‘critical safety incidents’ and ‘catastrophic risk’ activities (European Parliament and
Council, 2024; California State Legislature, 2025b). These instruments set out requirements for which AI incidents
require escalation, when they must be reported, and to whom, though the severity thresholds for AI harms are not
always operationally clear or quantified. We begin by examining the AI harm taxonomies offered by these regulations
in relation to their roles in incident escalation. The harm thresholds within these two leading legislative instruments
inform the design of our international incident escalation framework.
3.2.1
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: the EU AI Act
The 2024 EU AI Act, hereafter EUAIA, is a regulatory expression of the European Commission’s 2019 Ethics Guidelines
for Trustworthy AI, developed by the independent High-Level Expert Group on AI, and also reflects the non-binding
European Declaration on Digital Rights and Principles for the Digital Decade (European Commission, 2019). On the
11


basis of regulating violations of these principles, the EUAIA offers escalation thresholds and trigger mechanisms for
the benefit of AI operators, intended ‘to ensure a consistent and high level of protection of public interests as regards
health, safety and fundamental rights’ (Recital 7) (European Parliament and Council, 2024). The Act further states that
a specific safeguard procedure should be established to ensure adequate and timely enforcement against AI systems
presenting a risk to health, safety, and fundamental rights, and that this should apply to high-risk AI systems and
prohibited systems that have been placed on the market, put into service, or used in violation of prohibited practices.
The following definitions build on these provisions.
The EU AI Act: AI systems.
The EU AI Act’s use of the term ‘operator’ is broad, covering a ‘provider’, ‘product
manufacturer’, ‘deployer’, the ‘authorized representative’ of a provider, an ‘importer’, or a ‘distributor’ involved in
the AI value chain (Art. 3(8)) (European Parliament and Council, 2024). Most notably, a ‘provider’ is the entity
that develops or places the AI system on the market (Art. 3(3)); a ‘deployer’ is a natural or legal person using an AI
system under its authority, except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal activity (Art. 3(4)); and a
‘distributor’ is an entity in the supply chain, other than the provider or importer, that makes an AI system available
on the market (Art. 3(7)). The EUAIA also distinguishes between an ‘AI model’ and an ‘AI system’: AI models are
essential components of AI systems, but do not in themselves constitute AI systems. They require the addition of further
components, such as a user interface, in order to become AI systems (Recital 97). The Act also lays out an overlapping
classification regime for general-purpose AI, including ‘high-impact capabilities’ systems and ‘high-risk’ AI systems.
Where a general-purpose AI model is integrated into or forms part of an AI system, that system should be considered a
general-purpose AI system if it has the capability to serve a variety of purposes (Recital 100), and where the integrated
model can competently perform a wide range of distinct tasks, is typically trained on large amounts of data, and may use
self-supervised, unsupervised, or reinforcement learning methods (Recital 97). By contrast, a ‘high-impact capabilities’
system refers to systems whose capabilities match or exceed those recorded in the most advanced general-purpose
AI models (Recital 111), for example where the cumulative amount of computation used for training exceeds 1025
floating-point operations (Art. 51(2)) or where the model has been made available to at least 10,000 registered business
users established in the Union (Annex XIII(f)) (European Parliament and Council, 2024). The floating-point operations
threshold may be adjusted over time to reflect technological and industrial change (Recital 111).
A ‘high-risk’ AI system refers to those AI systems that, in light of their intended purpose, pose a high risk of harm to
health, safety, or fundamental rights, taking into account both the severity of the possible harm and its probability of
occurrence (Recital 52). The high-risk domain list, risk-management requirements under Article 9, and the full catalog
of prohibited practices under Article 5 are set out in Appendix A.
The EU AI Act: AI risk types.
The EU AI Act defines AI risk as the combination of the probability of an occurrence
of harm and the severity of that harm (Art. 3(2)). It separates more significant AI risk into two main categories: ‘serious
incident’ and ‘systemic risk’. According to Article 3(49), a ‘serious incident’ is an incident or malfunction leading
to death or serious damage to health; serious and irreversible disruption of the management and operation of critical
infrastructure; infringements of fundamental rights; or serious damage to property or the environment (European
Parliament and Council, 2024).
According to Recital 110, ‘systemic risk’ includes actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects relating to major
accidents, disruption of critical sectors, serious consequences to public health and safety, consequences for democratic
processes, public and economic security, or the dissemination of illegal, false, or discriminatory content. These risks
may arise across the model lifecycle and are shaped by misuse, reliability, fairness, security, autonomy, access to tools,
novel or combined modalities, release and distribution strategies, and the potential to remove guardrails. Article 3(65)
further defines ‘systemic risk’ as a risk specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, where
those capabilities may have significant effects on the Union market, fundamental rights, or society as a whole, and can
propagate at scale across the value chain. A notable example is ‘loss of control’, described in Recital 110 as ‘unintended
issues of control’. This includes risks relating to misalignment with human intent in domains such as CBRN risks,
offensive cyber capabilities, the control of physical systems and critical infrastructure, self-replication, training other
models, harmful bias and discrimination, disinformation, privacy harms, and threats to democratic values and human
rights. Appendix 1.4 of Chapter 3 (Safety and Security) of the voluntary General-Purpose AI Code of Practice develops
this further, defining ‘loss of control’ as risks arising where humans lose the ability to reliably direct, modify, or shut
down a model, potentially as a result of misalignment, self-reasoning, self-improvement, deception, resistance to goal
modification, power-seeking behavior, or autonomously creating or improving AI systems (European Commission,
2025).
The Code of Practice also elaborates the definition of ‘systemic risk’, including risks of major accidents; disruption
to critical sectors or infrastructure; harms to public mental health, freedom of expression and information, non-
discrimination, privacy and data protection, the environment, non-human welfare, economic security, and democratic
12


processes; and risks from concentration of power and illegal, violent, hateful, radicalising, or false content, including
child sexual abuse material and non-consensual intimate imagery (European Commission, 2025). It further identifies
four specified systemic risk domains: CBRN, loss of control, cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.
The EU AI Act and the Digital Services Act.
The EU AI Act functions as an additional layer to other EU frameworks,
most notably the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and the Digital Services Act (DSA) (European
Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022c). The DSA is particularly relevant in the case of Very Large
Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs), where Recital 76 acknowledges their
societal and systemic risks and calls for the highest standard of due-diligence operations. These platforms are designated
‘very large’ on the basis of the number of active recipients, exceeding 45 million or 10% of the Union’s population in
the relevant year.
When AI systems or GPAI models are embedded into or provide intermediary services for VLOPs or VLOSEs, those
AI systems become subject to the systemic risk-management framework established under Articles 33–35 of the DSA.
Article 34 mandates annual risk assessments, including risks arising from embedded AI systems and potential misuse.
This creates one possible data source for pattern detection, as recurring AI-related incidents across platforms with very
large user bases could, in principle, be surfaced through periodic risk assessment.
The DSA’s annual reporting cadence is also too slow for real-time incident clustering. It produces a periodic risk picture
rather than a real-time trigger when a pattern of sub-threshold events reaches a collective severity threshold. These
assessments are also platform-scoped rather than model-scoped, since Article 34 applies to the deployment layer, not
the model layer. A manipulation campaign arising from a frontier model and propagating through multiple platforms
could therefore generate multiple uncoordinated Article 34 assessments, without any clear obligation on the model
provider to contribute to or integrate them. The combined EUAIA/DSA architecture therefore risks fragmentation: a
model provider may report under Article 73 of the EUAIA if a serious incident threshold is crossed, while a platform
separately assesses systemic risk annually under Article 34 of the DSA, yet no binding mechanism requires these
assessments to be integrated, shared, or compared at the AI Office or Commission level. Further detail on the DSA
provisions, including Article 40 data access mechanisms, Article 48 crisis protocols, and Article 36 crisis-response
powers, is provided in Appendix A.
The EU AI Act: incident escalation requirements.
Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
with systemic risk to undertake serious incident reporting are set out in Articles 55 and 73 of the EUAIA. Under
Article 55(1)(c), providers must keep track of and report, without undue delay, relevant information about serious
incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office, and to national competent authorities where appropriate
(European Parliament and Council, 2024). Recital 114 emphasizes the importance of post-market monitoring and
recommends cooperation with relevant actors along the AI value chain.
Under the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, incident escalation requirements include systemic risk estimation,
which may involve qualitative risk scoring (Measure 3.4), and obligations under Commitment 9 on serious incident
reporting. Commitment 9 requires signatories to implement processes and measures for keeping track of and reporting
relevant information about serious incidents throughout the model lifecycle (European Commission, 2025). The detailed
reporting fields under Measures 9.1–9.2 and reporting timelines under Measure 9.3 are set out in Appendix A.
Measure 9.2 information remains tied to serious incident reporting and does not constitute a standalone near-miss
reporting channel. Points 8 and 9 of Measure 9.2 are excluded from the more immediate guidance on reporting
timelines under Measure 9.3, meaning that near misses may only be reported every four weeks in the case of unresolved
serious incidents, or in a final report submitted up to 60 days after resolution. Near-miss events may therefore reach
the AI Office more quickly through Safety and Security Framework updates or Model Report updates than through
serious incident reporting itself, raising the question of whether these are the appropriate reporting channels when both
depend on provider-assessed materiality thresholds. This gap is consequential for the highest-priority risk domains,
because the current regulatory architecture leaves reporting of near-miss signals subject to the discretion of the actor
with the strongest commercial incentive to assess them as non-material. In addition, because Article 3(49) defines
serious incidents in terms of a single event producing threshold-level harm, the binding text contains no provision for
classifying a pattern of individually sub-threshold incidents as collectively constituting a serious incident or systemic
risk trigger. There is no formal rolling window, no minimum number of correlated events that triggers an obligation,
and no mechanism for generating a cross-developer view of correlated incidents.
Another gap concerns reversibility. While irreversibility is explicitly named as a qualifying criterion for one serious
incident category—critical infrastructure disruption under Article 3(49)(b)—it does not function as a universal severity
modifier or independent escalation trigger across all harm types. Likewise, propagation potential—the likelihood, speed,
and pathway through which an incident may spread across systems, jurisdictions, or populations—is not a formal
13


criterion in Article 73 or in the serious incident definition. An incident that causes limited immediate harm but has high
propagation potential therefore does not trigger reporting on that basis alone. The overlapping architecture with the
Digital Services Act only partially addresses this gap, and only for models or systems within its scope. Article 36 of the
DSA establishes a crisis-response mechanism that enables the Commission to require mitigation measures from VLOPs
and VLOSEs where a serious threat to public security or public health has arisen. This is propagation-aware in the
sense that it is designed for situations in which harm is spreading faster than routine regulatory response can address.
However, Article 36 is reactive and Commission-initiated: it responds to crises already in progress, rather than enabling
pre-emptive escalation when propagation indicators are first detected. The crisis protocols under Article 48 also remain
voluntary and under-specified.
There are several further limitations to the effectiveness of Article 73. In cases where AI systems present risks
to health, safety, or fundamental rights, providers must ‘immediately investigate’ and inform market surveillance
authorities (Art. 20), but adequately operationalizing these risks remains underdeveloped. Forty-eight-hour reporting
is mandatory only in the case of ‘serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical
infrastructure’ (Art. 73(3)); reporting timelines are otherwise slower under Article 73(2) and (4). Reporting timelines
under Measure 9.3 of the Code of Practice are not faster than those under Article 73, except for serious cybersecurity
breaches, including model-weight exfiltration and cyberattacks, where signatories establish or suspect with ‘reasonable
likelihood’ a causal relationship between their model and the breach, in which case reporting is expected within five
days (European Commission, 2025). Article 73 also excludes systems not designated as high-risk, as well as forms of
AI hazard in which serious harm could plausibly occur without yet having done so, both of which any incident threshold
design must address.
3.2.2
California Senate Bill 53: thresholds, gaps, and comparisons
The 2025 California Senate Bill 53 (SB 53) enacts the Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (TFAIA). It is
significantly more succinct than the EUAIA, but introduces a distinct set of AI harm definitions and thresholds intended
to respond to advances in frontier model capabilities and the potential catastrophic risks they may pose (California State
Legislature, 2025b).
SB 53 distinguishes between ‘frontier’ models and ‘foundation’ models. A foundation model must be trained on a
broad data set, designed for generality of output, and adaptable to a wide range of distinct tasks. A frontier model is, by
contrast, a foundation model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 1026 integer or floating-point
operations, including the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other material
modifications. The Act also distinguishes between a ‘frontier developer’ and a ‘large frontier developer’, the latter being
a developer whose annual gross revenues, together with those of its affiliates, exceed $500,000,000 in the preceding
calendar year.
‘Catastrophic risk’ is defined as a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer’s development, storage, use, or
deployment of a foundation or frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than
50 people, or more than one billion dollars in damage to, or loss of, property, arising from a single incident involving a
frontier model. The qualifying activities include providing expert-level assistance in the creation or release of a CBRN
weapon; engaging in conduct with no meaningful human oversight that constitutes a cyberattack or, if committed by
a human, would constitute murder, assault, extortion, or theft; or evading the control of its frontier developer or user.
Section 1(j) further defines catastrophic risk as including both malicious uses and malfunctions, including AI-enabled
hacking, biological attacks, and loss of control (California State Legislature, 2025b).
Large frontier developers must also publish summaries of their catastrophic-risk assessments and the results of those
assessments before, or concurrently with, deploying a new frontier model or a substantially modified version of an
existing frontier model. Despite its breadth, the EUAIA does not provide a separate harm category for ‘catastrophic
risk’; SB 53’s definitions of ‘critical safety incidents’ would therefore, in many cases, fall across both serious incidents
and systemic risks under the EU framework. However, SB 53 also introduces carve-outs to catastrophic risk. These
include information output by a model that is otherwise publicly accessible in substantially similar form from another
source; lawful activity of the federal government; and harms caused by a model in combination with other software
where the model did not materially contribute to the harm. These carve-outs require careful treatment in any incident
escalation trigger design.
‘Critical safety incidents’ under SB 53 are defined to include: unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of
model weights resulting in death or bodily injury; harm resulting from the materialisation of a catastrophic risk; loss of
control of a foundation model causing death or bodily injury; or a foundation model using deceptive techniques against
the frontier developer to subvert controls or monitoring, outside the context of an evaluation designed to elicit that
behavior, in a manner that demonstrates materially increased catastrophic risk (California State Legislature, 2025b).
These definitions are framed around single incidents. Accordingly, SB 53 contains no correlated-incident aggregation
14


provision and no temporal clustering mechanism for capturing patterns of individually sub-threshold incidents that
collectively amount to catastrophic risk.
The OES reporting mechanism, frontier framework requirements, and associated reporting timelines are set out in
Appendix A.
Several structural gaps in SB 53’s escalation and reporting architecture nevertheless warrant attention. As with the
EUAIA, the absence of any correlated-incident aggregation mechanism is one of the most significant gaps. No temporal
clustering provision exists to capture patterns of related incidents, and the annual OES report uses anonymized and
aggregated data, limiting its usefulness for cross-incident pattern detection. The requirement to report critical safety
incidents within 15 days of discovery is also long relative to the pace at which AI-enabled harms may propagate,
especially in offensive cyber contexts. The absence of obligations for near misses, hazard reporting, and reversibility as
an assessment dimension compounds this problem. There is no provision for escalating a sub-threshold incident on the
basis that the harm, if realized, would be irreversible.
Catastrophic-risk carve-outs also create additional escalation gaps that must be consciously addressed in incident
threshold design. In particular, the exclusion of harms caused by a model ‘in combination with other software’ where
the model did not materially contribute to the harm is problematic for cases of embedded infrastructure, where harm
arises from AI behavior within a multi-component pipeline rather than from direct autonomous action. The qualitative
threshold as to whether a model has ‘materially contributed’ also introduces causal ambiguity that escalation architecture
should encode explicitly. The voluntary nature of foundation-model reporting under §22757.13(c)(4) must likewise
be addressed. The distinction between frontier and foundation models means that a significant category of deployed
AI systems—those below the frontier threshold but still capable of contributing to serious harm when weaponized or
embedded in adversarial infrastructure—falls outside the mandatory reporting regime. Finally, the flexibility afforded to
large frontier developers to substitute their own ‘reasonable schedule’ for quarterly catastrophic-risk assessments under
§22757.12(d) further weakens the limited aggregation function that the annual OES report might otherwise serve.
In summary, the differing threshold designs of the EU AI Act and SB 53 show that harmonising international approaches
to AI governance remains challenging. Divergent harm thresholds and red lines across the two frameworks create
practical limitations that must be addressed when designing incident escalation triggers intended to capture both.
3.3
Incident response in other domains

determinations are made as to when risks are considered severe or systemic enough to warrant international escalation.
The aim is not to provide an exhaustive comparison, but to identify transferable design patterns from established incident
response frameworks that may be applicable to AI incident escalation.

3.3.2
Sendai Framework and the IASC Scale-Up Activation
The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 was adopted at the Third UN World Conference on
Disaster Risk Reduction on 18 March 2015 and endorsed by the UN General Assembly shortly thereafter (United
Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, 2015). The Framework sets the structure within which humanitarian
escalation decisions are taken, with global targets and priorities for action that Member States use to calibrate national
and international response capacity. The framework includes a mechanism for System-Wide Scale-Up Activation
in response to crises meeting a five-criterion threshold: scale, urgency, complexity, capacity, and risk of failure
(Inter-Agency Standing Committee, 2018). Activation moves international agencies from their normal capacity and
coordination structures into a mandatory surge regime of accelerated funding, senior leadership deployment, and
centralized crisis coordination. A 2018 reform replaced the earlier tiered “L1/L2/L3” labels with a single binary
decision: Scale-Up or not (Inter-Agency Standing Committee, 2018).
3.3.3
International Health Regulations and the PHEIC architecture
The International Health Regulations (2005) were adopted by the 58th World Health Assembly on 23 May 2005 and
entered into force on 15 June 2007 (World Health Organization, 2005). Their purpose, set out in Article 2, is “to prevent,
protect against, control and provide a public health response to the international spread of disease in ways that are
commensurate with and restricted to public health risks, and which avoid unnecessary interference with international
traffic and trade” (World Health Organization, 2005). The IHR are the most mature international incident-notification
regime in existence and have served as a reference architecture for several of the more recent instruments discussed
below.
The IHR address four distinct design questions: what threshold triggers escalation, how that threshold is assessed, how
quickly notification must follow, and how much causal certainty is required. The threshold condition—a public health
emergency of international concern (PHEIC)—is defined as an extraordinary event that constitutes a public health
risk to other States through international disease spread and may require a coordinated international response (World
Health Organization, 2005). To assess whether an event meets this threshold, National Focal Points apply four questions
16


covering seriousness, unusualness, risk of international spread, and risk of travel or trade restrictions; two “yes” answers
trigger mandatory notification. Four named diseases—smallpox, wild-type poliovirus, novel-subtype human influenza,
and SARS—bypass the assessment entirely and are always notifiable. Once an event is assessed, States have a hard
24-hour notification window. Critically, the assessment does not require confirmed cause: it asks whether the event is
“caused by or associated with” a listed disease or novel pathogen, recognizing that attribution is often incomplete when
escalation decisions must be taken.
3.3.4
NIS2, the CSIRTs Network and EU-CyCLONe
Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2) was adopted on 14 December 2022 and established a transposition deadline of
17 October 2024 (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022b). It replaces the earlier NIS1 Directive
(Directive (EU) 2016/1148), which had established the EU CSIRTs Network under Article 12 (European Parliament
and Council of the European Union, 2016). NIS2 significantly expands the sectoral scope, tightens incident-reporting
timelines, and introduces a formal operational-level crisis-coordination body, EU-CyCLONe.
NIS2 defines scope by enumerating covered sectors, including energy, transport, banking, health, and digital infrastruc-
ture, while explicitly excluding national security, defense, and law-enforcement activities (European Parliament and
Council of the European Union, 2022b). The escalation trigger is a two-part test: an incident qualifies as significant
where it has caused or could cause severe operational disruption or financial loss, or has affected or could affect other
persons through material or non-material damage. Because this test applies to any entity in a covered sector, sectoral
classification itself acts as a first-stage filter: a significant incident at a covered entity is reportable without further
severity screening.
Once triggered, NIS2 imposes a three-stage notification timeline: early warning within 24 hours, incident notification
within 72 hours, and a final report within one month. Harm is tracked across four categories: availability, authenticity,
integrity, and confidentiality of data or services, and entities are required to maintain business continuity and disaster
recovery capabilities, making recoverability an operational obligation rather than merely a reporting field.
For cross-border escalation, NIS2 establishes EU-CyCLONe, activated when an incident exceeds a single Member
State’s response capacity or significantly impacts two or more Member States. This sits within a three-tier structure:
technical response (CSIRTs Network), operational crisis coordination (CyCLONe), and political response (IPCR)
(European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022b).
3.3.5
DORA: digital operational resilience in the EU financial sector
DORA addresses operational rather than purely cyber risk in the EU financial sector, and is a detailed threshold-based
escalation framework currently in force (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022a). Like the
IHR, DORA does not require attribution to a specific threat actor: classification and reporting turn on the occurrence and
consequences of an ICT-related incident, rather than on identifying who caused it (European Parliament and Council of
the European Union, 2022a, Arts. 17–20).
Incidents are classified against six criteria: number of clients or financial counterparts affected, duration, geographical
spread, data losses, criticality of affected services, and economic impact (European Commission, 2024). An incident is
classified as major where it affects a critical service and meets concrete materiality thresholds, for example, more than
10% of clients or more than 100,000 affected, duration exceeding 24 hours, spread across two or more Member States,
or economic impact exceeding EUR 100,000, as detailed in Article 8 (European Commission, 2024, Art. 8). Notably,
these thresholds combine technical indicators of what went wrong with measures of downstream impact, assessing both
within a single classification system (European Commission, 2024).
DORA also includes a related-incident aggregation rule: individually sub-threshold incidents that share the same
apparent root cause and collectively meet the classification criteria within a rolling six-month window are deemed
major, and entities must assess for such patterns monthly (European Commission, 2024). DORA also distinguishes
system-level recoverability from harm-level reversibility: entities must set and test Recovery Time Objectives and
Recovery Point Objectives for each function, but these measure how quickly systems and data can be restored, not
whether downstream consequences can be reversed (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022a).
For cross-border coordination, major incidents are reported to competent authorities, with onward transmission within
the EU supervisory architecture, including to the ESAs and, where relevant, the ECB (European Parliament and Council
of the European Union, 2022a).

3.3.6
FSB, Basel III and the G-SIB assessment
The Financial Stability Board, established at the 2009 London G20 summit and hosted by the Bank for International
Settlements, has the mandate to “coordinate at the international level the work of national financial authorities and
international standard-setting bodies and develop . . . effective regulatory, supervisory and other financial sector policies
in the interest of financial stability” (Financial Stability Board, 2012). While the FSB does not operate an incident-
notification regime, it is responsible for identifying institutions and activities whose distress or failure would threaten
systemic stability.
The methodology it uses is an indicator-based scoring approach across five equally weighted categories: size, intercon-
nectedness, substitutability and financial-institution infrastructure, complexity, and cross-jurisdictional activity. Banks
with a total Basel III leverage-exposure measure exceeding EUR 200 billion are included in the assessment sample
(Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2013). This illustrates an alternative approach to event-based notification:
upfront classification of the entity itself as systemic, with elevated capital requirements, resolution planning, and
supervisory scrutiny attaching to classification rather than to any particular incident.
3.3.7
Basel II operational risk: event taxonomy and near-miss treatment
The Basel II operational-risk framework provides a developed international taxonomy for loss-event classification. It
defines operational risk as the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems, or
from external events, and categorizes loss events into seven types: internal fraud, external fraud, employment practices
and workplace safety, clients/products/business practices, damage to physical assets, business disruption and system
failures, and execution/delivery/process management (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2006).
Alongside this taxonomy, Basel II set an explicit severity benchmark: banks’ internal risk models must be calibrated to
a 99.9th percentile confidence interval over a one-year period, meaning the model must capture what would happen
in the worst 0.1% of cases (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2011b). This remains the standard tail-risk
benchmark in banking supervision, and is the clearest example in international regulation of a threshold defined by
statistical severity rather than by event description.
On near misses, the Basel Committee’s Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk (BCBS 195) require
banks to supplement actual loss data with scenario analysis and to treat near-miss events as relevant inputs to risk
measurement even where they do not generate a recorded financial loss (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision,
2011a). Near misses feed into scenario analysis rather than directly into capital calculations: they inform understanding
of how often hazard conditions arise, without needing to have caused actual harm.
3.3.8
IAEA: early notification and the INES severity scale
The nuclear regime was built in direct response to crisis. The IAEA’s Convention on Early Notification of a Nuclear
Accident was adopted five months after the Chernobyl accident in 1986 (International Atomic Energy Agency, 1986).
Its escalation trigger is not a severity threshold but a propagation condition: States must notify the IAEA of any nuclear
accident whose radiological consequences could cross a national boundary, regardless of how severe the incident is
domestically.
The severity-classification element came four years later with the International Nuclear and Radiological Event Scale
(INES), a seven-level scale from Anomaly (Level 1) to Major Accident (Level 7) (International Atomic Energy Agency,
2019). Importantly, INES is used for public communication rather than as a legal reporting trigger: notification
obligations still turn on the transboundary test. The nuclear regime thus decouples the decision to escalate from the
severity rating, whereas NIS2, DORA, and the IHR integrate them more closely.
3.3.9
ICAO Annex 13/19 and Seveso III: near misses and the no-blame principle
Civil aviation and major industrial-accident regimes jointly provide the most developed precedent for near-miss
reporting. ICAO Annex 13 governs aircraft accident and incident investigation; paragraph 3.1 of Chapter 3 states: “The
sole objective of the investigation of an accident or incident shall be the prevention of accidents and incidents. It is
not the purpose of this activity to apportion blame or liability” (International Civil Aviation Organization, 2024). This
no-blame principle has been essential to achieving the reporting rates needed to make near-miss data statistically useful;
without it, the incentive to report is dominated by the incentive to avoid liability.
ICAO Annex 19 builds the system-wide architecture around this: mandatory and voluntary reporting systems, State
Safety Programmes, and operator-level Safety Management Systems together provide the formal infrastructure for
treating near misses as important data (International Civil Aviation Organization, 2016).
