The closest analogue outside aviation is the Seveso III Directive on major-accident hazards involving dangerous
substances (UK Health and Safety Executive, 2025). Seveso III is notable for two design choices. First, obligations are
triggered by what a facility handles—substance-quantity thresholds—rather than by something having gone wrong,
meaning scope is determined before any incident occurs. Second, the reporting regime explicitly covers near misses
(“dangerous occurrences”) alongside actual accidents, establishing the principle that hazard indicators, not just realized
harms, warrant systematic collection and international aggregation.
3.3.10
Metrics used for propagation in other domains
Several of the frameworks above use quantitative metrics for how fast an incident spreads and how quickly it is detected.
Reproduction numbers.
In epidemiology, the basic reproduction number R0 measures how many secondary in-
fections a single case produces in a fully susceptible population; the effective reproduction number Re adjusts for
immunity, behavior change, and intervention (Anderson and May, 1991). An Re > 1 means the outbreak is growing; an
Re < 1 means it is shrinking. While the IHR do not explicitly name R0, their “significant risk of international spread”
criterion is in practice assessed using reproduction-number estimates.
Doubling time and serial interval.
Doubling time measures how quickly cumulative cases double; the serial interval
measures the time between successive cases in a transmission chain (Anderson and May, 1991). These are speed
metrics: they describe not whether propagation is occurring, but how fast.
Breakout time.
In cybersecurity, breakout time is the interval from initial compromise to the first lateral movement
into the wider network (CrowdStrike, n.d.). It defines the minimum window defenders have to detect and contain an
intrusion before it expands, and is the cyber equivalent of the serial interval: a speed metric rather than a severity metric.
MTTD and MTTR.
Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Respond (MTTR) help determine how far an
incident spreads before it is addressed. Two cases illustrate why both matter. In the SolarWinds campaign, attackers
maintained access for approximately fourteen months before discovery, during which compromised updates propagated
to roughly 18,000 organizations: a long, undetected spread (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, 2021).
NotPetya, by contrast, was designed for near-simultaneous detonation across shared infrastructure, with global damages
exceeding USD 10 billion: no detection window existed because the propagation pathway was effectively instantaneous
(Greenberg, 2018). The common thread is that propagation potential alone can be an escalation-relevant signal,
independent of realized harm.
3.3.11
Incident typologies
Incident typologies refer to the structures that frameworks use to classify incidents. These structures matter because
harm manifests in different ways: as acute, discrete events in some cases, and as diffuse or cumulative patterns across
affected populations in others. The classification approach therefore determines which incident types an escalation
framework will detect and escalate. Across the domains reviewed, four broad distinctions recur.
Event-based versus loss-based framings (what happened vs. what was lost).
Some regimes treat the unit of
escalation as a discrete event, for example an outbreak, a release, or an accident, where severity is judged by the nature
of the event itself. Others, most notably Basel II, treat the unit as the realized financial loss, and classify the underlying
event only as a secondary step (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2006). NIS2 and DORA sit in between:
they describe incidents in event-based terms but use loss-based thresholds to decide when something counts as a major
incident, for example economic impact above EUR 100,000 or duration longer than 24 hours. For general-purpose
AI, a hybrid framing is likely to be appropriate: some incidents have a clear event structure, while others are better
characterized by how harm is distributed across many affected users.
Expected versus tail outcomes (routine risk vs. extraordinary risk).
Basel draws a line at the 99.9th percentile,
separating routine risk management from tail-risk management: what is likely to happen versus what would happen
only in the worst 0.1% of cases (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2011b). The same distinction carries over to
AI: everyday system errors are expected and managed day to day, while rare but catastrophic failures are a systemic-risk
problem requiring a different governance response. For routine risk, spikes in volumes can also indicate a more material
risk.
Frequency–severity decomposition (how often vs. how bad).
Operational-risk modeling treats frequency and
severity as separate questions. This is why near-miss reporting matters: a near miss produces no harm, but it still
19


indicates how often the conditions for harm are arising. Collecting near-miss data is, in effect, a way of using frequency
signals to sharpen estimates of what severe outcomes could look like (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision,
2011a).
Correlated, related, and single-event incidents.
Three distinct multi-incident patterns appear across the comparator
set, each requiring different handling. Single events are the default unit in the IHR and IAEA regimes. Related
events, defined as incidents sharing a common root cause, are aggregated explicitly under DORA within a rolling
six-month window (European Commission, 2024). Correlated events, defined as incidents without a shared root cause
but occurring under similar conditions or exposures, are addressed in frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK, where
individually low-severity observations may form steps in a coherent attack chain that is considerably more severe than
any single component (MITRE, n.d.b).
3.4
Current AI incident tracking and its challenges
Designing escalation criteria and triggers requires reliable incident data. In practice, however, the current landscape
of AI incident tracking presents two interrelated challenges. First, many AI incidents do not lend themselves to the
kind of clear, standardized classification that trigger systems depend on. Second, the data infrastructure used to capture
incidents has not been designed with operational escalation in mind. Together, these constraints limit how precisely and
reliably escalation thresholds can be defined and applied.
To ground what follows, consider a state-sponsored disinformation campaign in which AI-generated content is used to
flood information ecosystems across multiple countries. This is the scenario documented across Incidents 727, 884, 929
and 968 in the AIID.
Challenges intrinsic to the nature of AI incidents.
Temporal ambiguity. Many AI incidents have no clear start
or end date. Ongoing harms such as AI-generated disinformation campaigns are not isolated events but continuously
adapting phenomena (Paeth et al., 2024b). A trigger system must define when an incident begins in order to assess its
severity, but for cumulative or evolving harms, that boundary is often arbitrary. The Pravda campaign illustrates this
directly: the disinformation infrastructure predates its AI-assisted amplification by years, and no single incident in the
cluster has an unambiguous start date.
Multiplicity. A widely deployed AI system may produce thousands of essentially identical harm instances. The AI
Incident Database introduced “incident variants” to manage this, recording one incident per distinct failure mode with
variants for notable individual cases (McGregor et al., 2022b). But the choice of aggregation rule dramatically alters the
data, with the same underlying reality recorded as one serious incident or ten thousand minor ones. This has significant
implications for whether a severity threshold is crossed. In the Pravda case, each AI chatbot repeating a Kremlin-aligned
narrative could plausibly be recorded as a separate incident or as a variant of a single systemic failure; the aggregation
choice determines whether any threshold is met.
Causal attribution. The AIID uses a counterfactual “but-for” test: would the harm have occurred but for the AI
system? Paeth et al. (2024b) argue this is not merely practically difficult but inherently unknowable, and mistakenly
treats real and hypothetical data as equally valid. The AIID compensates by setting a low causal bar where AI need
only be a necessary link in the causal chain, not the primary cause, but this trades precision for coverage, admitting
incidents where the AI’s contribution ranges from marginal to decisive. Whether AI “caused” the harm in the Pravda
case or amplified a pre-existing propaganda infrastructure is precisely the kind of counterfactual that cannot be resolved
at the point of assessment.
Near-misses and probing behavior. Existing databases systematically exclude incidents that do not generate actualized
harm. The AIID explicitly filters out theoretical flaws and unrealized vulnerabilities (McGregor et al., 2022b); the
OECD folded near-misses into its broader “hazards” category because experts could not reliably distinguish them from
other non-harm events (OECD, 2026). This creates a structural blind spot for precisely the signals that may matter
most for long-term safety: an AI system that tests boundaries without crossing them, exhibiting probing behavior to
determine what it can access, what triggers oversight, and what goes unnoticed. This generates no recordable harm but
may constitute the most important early warning for loss-of-control trajectories which require international response.
Adversarial adaptation. Unlike the systems monitored in aviation or nuclear safety, advanced AI systems may
strategically adapt to avoid detection. Apollo Research identified “scheming” behavior, where models pursue alternative
objectives while appearing compliant (Meinke et al., 2024), and separate work has documented “sandbagging”, where
models deliberately underperform during capability evaluations (Weij et al., 2025). This means that evaluation-based
thresholds can be actively undermined by the systems they are designed to monitor, and that trigger reliability may
degrade as systems become more capable. The implication is that single-point capability evaluations are an insufficient
20


basis for escalation triggers, and that continuous monitoring for behavioral patterns across deployments is a design
necessity. This constraint is one motivation for the pattern-detection mechanism at Criterion 4.
Cross-incident pattern blindness. Current databases record individual incidents, but systemic risk often emerges
from correlations between incidents rather than their individual severity. Jeanmaire and Boger (2025) observe that a
prompt injection vulnerability in one company’s chatbot and a similar exploit in others appear unrelated unless someone
aggregates the data. A trigger system focused on single-incident thresholds could miss distributed attacks or convergent
failure modes. This is compounded by the unknown developer problem: over a third of recent incidents cannot be
attributed to a known AI developer (Booth, 2026), making it impossible to check whether seemingly unrelated incidents
share a common upstream cause. In the Pravda case, the link between Incidents 727, 884, 929 and 968 was established
through intelligence analysis and investigative journalism, not through anything visible in AI developer monitoring
systems. Without cross-incident visibility, the cluster would appear as four unrelated events.
Reporting bias. The data upon which any trigger system operates is self-reported and media-dependent. AIID
acknowledges that all global reporting represents only a fraction of the lived realities of those experiencing AI harms
(Booth, 2026). The OECD’s pipeline, despite processing over 150,000 articles daily (OECD, 2026), cannot verify the
accuracy of its sources and is skewed toward English-language outlets. This creates a two-sided distortion: sensational
incidents are over-represented, while gradual or invisible harms are under-represented. Discrimination incidents actually
decreased in 2025 reporting despite no evidence the underlying problem improved, suggesting reporting patterns
track media attention cycles rather than harm trajectories (Booth, 2026). For the Pravda campaign, systematic effects
in non-Anglophone countries would be substantially undercounted by any pipeline dependent on English-language
sources.
Contextual calibration. Even if standardisation were achievable in the abstract, a trigger calibrated for one jurisdiction’s
risk profile may be meaningless for another. A nation heavily dependent on AI-managed financial infrastructure has a
different exposure surface from one where primary AI deployment is in agriculture or public administration. Universal
triggers therefore carry the risk of leaving countries under- or over-protected, a challenge compounded by the geographic
and linguistic biases already identified in current reporting pipelines (Paeth et al., 2024b; OECD, 2026).
The reversibility of harm is treated as a distinct assessment dimension in Criterion 7 and the Irreversible Harm section
below.
Challenges in current data practice.
Sophisticated threshold frameworks from other domains depend on granular,
well-attributed incident data. In pharmaceutical regulation, adverse event reports are linked to specific drug formulations
and batch numbers, enabling rapid identification of product-level risk signals. AI incident data currently operates at a
level of attribution granularity closer to “a medicine caused harm” than to “batch #4721 of 50mg formulation X caused
harm.” The specific infrastructure gaps that produce this disparity are set out below.
Completeness. AI incident reporting is voluntary, unsystematic, and overwhelmingly media-dependent. The AIID
relies on crowd-sourced submissions filtered through editorial review; the OECD’s AIM Monitor processes news articles
from Event Registry. Neither receives structured reports from the entities best positioned to detect incidents: the AI
developers and deployers themselves. In financial services, by contrast, Basel II mandates that firms collect and report
internal loss data above defined thresholds, creating a dataset that is incomplete by design but systematically incomplete
in a way that can be modeled. AI incident data is arbitrarily incomplete: what gets captured depends on whether a
journalist noticed, whether a victim reported it, and whether the harm was visible enough to generate a news story.
Timeliness. The most automated existing pipeline, the OECD AIM Monitor, processes events from one to four days
after first registration, with a hard four-day window for article collection. Articles appearing later are likely to be
misclassified as a separate event, fragmenting the picture of evolving incidents. Most AIID entries are added weeks
or months after the incident occurred. For a trigger system intended to activate international response, this latency is
operationally disqualifying for fast-moving incidents. By comparison, financial transaction monitoring systems flag
suspicious activity in real time, and aviation incident reporting mandates initial notification within hours.
Structured severity data. Even where incidents are recorded, the vast majority lack the structured annotations a trigger
system would need. Only 214 of over 750 AIID incidents had received CSET AI Harm Taxonomy annotations, and
only 188 had GMF taxonomy classifications, at the time of Paeth et al.’s review (Paeth et al., 2024b). A trigger system
cannot query “show me all incidents involving physical harm to more than 1,000 people in critical infrastructure sectors”
against a database where most entries lack fields for harm type, affected population size, or sector. The MIT AI Risk
Repository found that severity coding had a 20% disagreement rate between LLM-classified and human-classified
ratings (Slattery et al., 2025), a margin unacceptable for operational trigger decisions.
Verification. No existing system independently verifies the accuracy of the incident reports it ingests. The OECD
explicitly states that it cannot guarantee and does not independently verify the accuracy, completeness, or validity
21


of third-party information. The AIID’s editors guide documents specific cognitive biases affecting human curation,
including entity bias, the tendency to accept allegations against disliked companies with insufficient evidence. In
domains where triggers have operational consequences, there are independent investigative bodies whose assessments
carry institutional authority precisely because they are verified. AI incident data currently lacks any equivalent
verification layer.
Data flow from developers. Perhaps the most consequential gap is that data does not flow from AI developers into
any public incident infrastructure. Developers hold privileged technical knowledge about model behavior, capability
evaluations, and internal safety incidents, creating systematic information asymmetry. Company frameworks such as
Anthropic’s RSP, OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, and DeepMind’s FSF generate internal incident and capability
data, but this remains proprietary. When incidents do enter public databases, they are typically stripped of the technical
detail (model version, system architecture, evaluation results) that would be most useful for severity classification.
The EU AI Act’s Article 73 mandates serious incident reporting for high-risk AI systems from August 2026, which
represents the first regulatory attempt to compel data flow, but its scope excludes general-purpose AI under the main
reporting obligation.
Attribution to specific systems. The attribution problem extends beyond unknown developers. Even where a developer
is identified, incidents are rarely linked to specific model versions, deployment configurations, or capability profiles.
The AIID lacks fields for application names; the AIAAIC lacks fields for affected parties (Agarwal and Nene, 2025). A
trigger system cannot answer questions essential for detecting systemic risk patterns: whether this is the same model
involved in a previous incident, or whether three seemingly separate incidents share a common upstream capability. In
pharmaceutical regulation, the equivalent questions are answered as a matter of routine; in AI incident data, they are
largely unanswerable.
These sub-problems interact and compound. The Pravda campaign brings them together in a single case: an ongoing
disinformation operation (temporal ambiguity) affecting millions of users across multiple countries (multiplicity)
where AI-generated content was one contributing factor among many (causal ambiguity), with incident linkages only
identifiable through intelligence sources outside any developer’s monitoring systems (cross-incident blindness), and
effects in non-Anglophone countries systematically undercounted (reporting bias), with no data flowing from affected
AI developers to any public registry (data flow gap). A trigger system must simultaneously determine when such an
incident started, how to count its harms, how much to attribute to AI, and how urgently to respond, with defensible
answers to none of these questions readily available.
These challenges directly shape the design choices in the eight criteria that follow. Temporal ambiguity and multiplicity
inform the causal confidence modifier at Criterion 1 and the rolling-window aggregation logic at Criterion 4. The
near-miss gap motivates the standalone treatment at Criterion 8. Adversarial adaptation, and its implication that
evaluation-based triggers are unreliable, is a further rationale for continuous pattern monitoring at Criterion 4. The
data infrastructure limitations, particularly the absence of cross-developer data flows, are why the methodology section
distinguishes between criteria assessable by individual providers and those that require a central coordinating body.
3.5
Propagation dynamics: from common exposure to network contagion
Risk propagation operates through three distinct mechanisms. Common exposure produces simultaneous failures
across entities sharing an upstream dependency without contagion between them; existing supply-chain frameworks are
broadly adequate (Rinaldi et al., 2001). Environmental coupling operates through a shared medium, for example in a
financial market where each participant’s actions alter the price all others respond to, creating amplifying feedback.
Perrow (Perrow, 1999) identified tight coupling and interactive complexity as preconditions for “normal accidents”
(failures inevitable from the system’s architecture), and Maas (Maas, 2018) showed AI deployments increasingly exhibit
these properties. Network contagion spreads failure entity-to-entity through direct connections. Watts (Watts, 2002)
showed threshold-based activation produces cascades only within a specific connectivity window; Pastor-Satorras and
Vespignani (Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani, 2001) showed single-contact transmission in scale-free networks faces no
effective epidemic threshold. These describe different regimes: some AI risks are single-contact (prompt injection),
others threshold-dependent (algorithmic collusion); the first demands hub protection, the second structural monitoring.
These dynamics are compounded by interdependence across network layers. Buldyrev et al. (Buldyrev et al., 2010)
showed interdependent networks undergo abrupt cascading collapse where isolated networks degrade gradually. Gai
and Kapadia (Gai and Kapadia, 2010) identified the “robust-yet-fragile” property: connections diversifying risk
normally become contagion channels under stress. Acemoglu et al. (Acemoglu et al., 2015) formalized the threshold
at which networks switch from shock-absorbing to shock-amplifying. Scheffer et al. (Scheffer et al., 2009) showed
that approaching critical transitions produce detectable early-warning signals, e.g. increasing autocorrelation, rising
variance, or flickering, enabling anticipatory intervention. Helbing (Helbing, 2013) synthesized these for globally
22


networked risks: contagion, feedback amplification, and cross-domain interdependence produce systemic vulnerabilities
no single jurisdiction can address.
For AI incidents, these mechanisms manifest as four operationally distinct propagation types. Supply-chain prop-
agation: a vulnerability in a widely-used model or platform is inherited by all downstream systems (Rinaldi et al.,
2001; Buldyrev et al., 2010; Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021). Capability propagation: the harmful capability itself is
replicated or transferred, for example through weight exfiltration, technique reproduction, or capability uplift, spreading
risk beyond the original context (Hammond et al., 2025). Emergent propagation: harm amplifies through use dynamics
rather than technical dependencies, producing outcomes not attributable to any individual system (Calvano et al., 2020;
Carichon et al., 2025). Finally, rate of propagation versus rate of control: when propagation outpaces containment, a
local concern becomes international regardless of pathway type, following the epidemiological logic in which sustained
spread requires only that transmission exceed recovery (Gu et al., 2024; Kirilenko et al., 2017). An incident may
progress through multiple types in sequence, with the rate comparison determining at each stage whether containment
remains feasible.
3.5.1
Propagation in regulated domains
Several mature regulatory domains have developed operational frameworks for managing propagation risk, providing
both institutional vocabulary and structural precedents for AI-specific governance.
Financial stability regulation offers the most developed treatment. The Basel Committee’s framework for identifying
systemically important banks uses interconnectedness as a primary indicator, recognizing that shared exposures create
correlated risk invisible to institution-level supervision (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2013). The 2010
Flash Crash demonstrated this operationally: a single large sell order interacted with algorithmically similar trading
strategies to produce a feedback cascade that briefly erased nearly one trillion US dollars in market value within fifteen
minutes (Kirilenko et al., 2017). The regulatory response — market-wide circuit breakers that halt trading when price
movements exceed defined thresholds — directly implements cascade-interruption logic. The European Systemic Risk
Board’s 2025 report extends this analysis explicitly to AI, identifying foundation model concentration, algorithmic
monoculture, and AI-driven herding as novel systemic risk channels (European Systemic Risk Board Advisory Scientific
Committee, 2025).
In critical infrastructure protection, DORA and NIS2 establish mandatory incident classification, reporting timelines, and
cross-border coordination for ICT-related disruptions in financial services and essential services respectively (European
Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022a,b). DORA requires classification against defined impact criteria,
geographic reach, duration, affected clients, with significant incidents reported within strict timescales. NIS2 extends
comparable obligations across energy, transport, health, and digital infrastructure, with EU-CyCLONe providing
coordination when incidents affect two or more Member States. These frameworks demonstrate that propagation-based
escalation triggers are already operational: what elevates an incident from routine to significant is its capacity to
propagate across entities, sectors, or borders.
Cyber incident response provides a third model. CSIRT networks coordinate cross-border containment through
established protocols for sharing indicators of compromise (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), n.d.).
The CrowdStrike outage of July 2024, which was a single faulty update simultaneously disabling approximately 8.5
million Windows devices worldwide, demonstrated both the strengths and limitations: effective technical coordination,
but a propagation mechanism (common upstream dependency) outside the adversarial threat model CERT protocols are
optimized for (Microsoft, 2024).
The common structural feature across these domains is that escalation triggers are defined by observable downstream
impact rather than upstream causal mechanisms. This is appropriate when the cause-effect relationship is well
understood but it is inadequate when the causal mechanisms are novel, opaque, or qualitatively unprecedented, but these
are precisely the conditions AI regulators will find themselves in as AI continues to be developed and deployed. Existing
frameworks catch AI incidents (OECD, 2024a) when they manifest as specific infrastructure disruptions in particular
regulatory domains not specific to AI, such as DORA (financial entities), NIS2 (cybersecurity), or CyCLONe (critical
digital and communications infrastructure). Consequently, they do not catch AI-driven harms that are unique to AI and
do not fit domain-specific harm criteria, such as algorithmic collusion, cooperation failures, or emergent escalation, that
can generate significant harm without triggering infrastructure disruption thresholds. The Bletchley/Seoul/Paris summit
process recognizes these risk categories but has not translated them into operational triggers with defined thresholds,
mandatory notification, or response protocols (International AI Safety Report, 2026).
23


3.5.2
Cross-border propagation and governance triggers
International coordination becomes necessary when the scope of an incident’s interaction dynamics exceeds the
governance capacity of any single jurisdiction (Helbing, 2013). This structural mismatch is not primarily about harm
severity — a high-severity incident within one jurisdiction’s capacity is a domestic matter. It concerns whether any
single authority can observe the full incident, attribute responsibility, and implement effective containment.
The mismatch can manifest along three important dimensions.
Observational mismatch: no single regulator sees the full scope. An AI system trained in one jurisdiction, deployed
in a second, and producing effects in a third presents fragments to each authority. In multi-agent settings, interaction
dynamics spanning borders through shared environments may be invisible to any observation point. The OECD’s
work on AI incident definitions highlights that even identifying what constitutes a single incident becomes difficult
when causal chains cross organizational and jurisdictional boundaries (OECD, 2024a). The ESRB also identifies
model uniformity as a source of correlated financial behavior across institutions that amplifies systemic risk (European
Systemic Risk Board Advisory Scientific Committee, 2025).
Enforcement mismatch: the authority that can observe may lack jurisdiction to act, and vice versa. The EU AI Act
applies primarily to systems placed on the EU market or affecting EU persons, leaving gaps for externally hosted systems
whose effects propagate inward (European Parliament and Council, 2024). NIS2 and DORA coordinate within the Union
but not with non-EU jurisdictions. The Bletchley/Seoul/Paris commitments are voluntary and lack specified activation
thresholds (International AI Safety Report, 2026). For multi-agent incidents, enforcement mismatch compounds with
cross-domain fragmentation: an incident spanning financial markets, telecommunications, and information platforms
falls between multiple regulators’ mandates even domestically.
Temporal mismatch: the incident develops faster than institutional response. Circuit breakers in financial markets
exist because feedback-driven cascades develop on timescales precluding deliberative response (Kirilenko et al.,
2017). AI-mediated propagation exhibits the same asymmetry: adversarial content can spread through LLM agent
networks in logarithmic time (Gu et al., 2024), while cross-border coordination operates on timescales of hours to days.
When propagation outpaces coordination, containment depends on pre-positioned automatic mechanisms rather than
institutional deliberation.
A further challenge specific to AI-mediated propagation is that the relationship between cause and effect may confound
established attribution. In conventional cross-border incidents, the causal structure belongs to a known category;
attribution is difficult but conceptually defined. In incidents where harm arises from interaction dynamics rather than
any single system’s action, attribution may be structurally impossible as the harm is a property of the interaction,
not of any participant (Hammond et al., 2025). The 2010 Flash Crash remains contested on attribution fifteen years
later because the cascade was an emergent property of algorithmic interaction (Kirilenko et al., 2017). For emergent
multi-agent incidents, this may require reconceptualising responsibility from identifying which actor caused harm to
identifying which structural conditions enabled it.
Existing cross-border mechanisms are either operationally robust but not tailored to AI (DORA, NIS2, CyCLONe
catch AI incidents only incidentally), or AI-specific but operationally underdeveloped (Bletchley/Seoul/Paris lack
binding thresholds and response protocols). The intersection of: mandatory, AI-specific, and international, remains
undeveloped (International AI Safety Report, 2026). The severity threshold framework developed in this work is
intended to fill this gap.
3.5.3
Multi-agent risk amplification
The propagation mechanisms described above apply to any networked technology. Multi-agent AI systems do not
introduce new propagation mechanisms, but they introduce amplification mechanisms that can accelerate, extend, or
qualitatively transform propagation in ways single-system deployments do not (Hammond et al., 2025).
The first is the creation of correlated failure surfaces. When independently deployed AI systems share upstream
dependencies, they exhibit correlated vulnerabilities not visible at the individual deployment level. Kleinberg and
Raghavan (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021) formalized this as algorithmic monoculture: shared models produce
correlated errors that concentrate rather than diversify risk. Bommasani et al. (Bommasani et al., 2022) demonstrated
empirically that foundation model convergence leads to outcome homogenisation. Monoculture transforms the failure
distribution from independently distributed (self-limiting) to positively correlated across the entire dependent population,
with the shared dependency potentially invisible to deployers, regulators, or the agents themselves.
The second is emergent coordination through interaction. When multiple AI agents interact within a shared en-
vironment, their collective behavior can produce outcomes no individual agent was designed to produce. Calvano
et al. (Calvano et al., 2020) showed that reinforcement learning agents in pricing games consistently discover supra-
24


competitive pricing through endogenous signals alone, without communication or instructions to collude. Motwani et
al. (Motwani et al., 2024) demonstrated that LLM agents can develop steganographic channels enabling covert coordi-
nation while evading monitoring. Emergent coordination transforms environmental coupling into a self-reinforcing
feedback loop in such a way that agents’ responses alter the environment that further reinforces the coordinated behavior.
Once established, the emergent equilibrium is highly stable and disrupting it requires altering the interaction structure,
not remediating any individual agent. Rivera et al. (Rivera et al., 2024) demonstrated a parallel dynamic in military
simulations, where LLM agents exhibit difficult-to-predict escalation patterns emerging from interaction rather than
individual disposition.
The third and most dangerous mechanism is the transition from correlated exposure to emergent coordination. Gu
et al. (Gu et al., 2024) showed that a single adversarial image can compromise up to one million multimodal LLM agents
whereby each compromised agent propagates the attack to its neighbours. Ju et al. (Ju and others, 2024) demonstrated
that manipulated knowledge injected into one agent persists and amplifies through retrieval-augmented generation, with
downstream agents treating false information as verified fact. Carichon et al. (Carichon et al., 2025) argue this reflects a
fundamental property: alignment is a dynamic social process that degrades through interaction, such that individually
aligned agents converge on collectively misaligned equilibria. In each case, propagation begins as single-contact or
common-exposure but is amplified by interaction dynamics into a self-sustaining crisis.
These mechanisms intensify each governance challenge identified above. Correlated failure surfaces deepen obser-
vational mismatch and the shared dependency may be invisible to any single jurisdiction. Emergent coordination
deepens the attribution problem such that responsibility dissolves when harm is introduced via interaction dynamics.
The correlation-to-emergence transition deepens temporal mismatch and increases the risk from multi-agent feedback,
amplifying vulnerabilities faster than institutional responses can manage. Detection requires monitoring interaction
properties between agents, not individual agents and this is a challenge for which statistical and information-theoretic
approaches provide a foundation (Harré, 2022; Scheffer et al., 2009), but which remains largely unimplemented in
operational governance.
3.6
Irreversible harm and the logic of escalation
When an AI incident produces harm that cannot practically be reversed there is a qualitative change in the governance
response needed. Reversible harm is ultimately a question of resources: who pays, how long will recovery take, and
whether the responsible actor has the capacity to restore the system to the pre-incident state. Irreversible harm closes off
that recovery path. In that case the cost of restoration is essentially undefined and the response must shift from recovery
coordination to impact management. This section reviews how existing frameworks treat irreversibility, why those
treatments are inadequate for AI incidents, and what foundations from adjacent domains support the layered assessment
structure adopted in the present framework.
Existing AI governance instruments treat irreversibility as a property of harm type rather than as an independent
assessment dimension. The EU AI Act names irreversibility as a qualifying criterion for critical infrastructure disruption
(Article 3(49)(b)) and the GPAI Code of Practice makes it definitional for loss of control risk, defined as situations
where regaining control is “either extremely costly or impossible.” But an incident producing moderate yet permanently
irreversible harm to fundamental rights, property, or the environment has no accelerated escalation pathway under the
Act on the basis of its irreversibility alone. California’s SB 53 does not mention reversibility explicitly; its threshold
structure assumes that harm type and magnitude are sufficient for classification. The irreversibility embedded in its
harm outcomes, e.g. death, or bodily injury, is classified by the nature of the incident, not by recoverability. The
Bletchley/Seoul/Paris declarations reference catastrophic and irreversible risk but provide no operational definition of
what irreversibility might mean in practice, and consequently no escalation trigger is covered.
These limitations become apparent when applied to AI incidents where the question is not whether harm is irreversible
but at what level and on what timescale irreversibility is measured. A training data poisoning incident may be technically
containable (the data source can be blocked) while the model weights are permanently compromised (retraining is the
only remedy) and the downstream societal effects (public trust in AI-generated information) are unrecoverable on any
feasible timescale. Such a binary framing of irreversibility cannot address these issues. What is needed, and what is
proposed here, is a decomposition of recovery into distinct phases, each with its own assessment criteria and temporal
characteristics.
The theoretical foundations for this decomposition are well established in environmental economics, where the
interaction between irreversibility and uncertainty has been a central concern since Arrow and Fisher (1974). They
showed that when an action may produce irreversible environmental damage and the consequences are uncertain, the
expected net benefit of the action is reduced by what they termed the quasi-option value: the value of preserving the
option to act differently once better information is available. This was later formalized by Hanemann (1989) as a
25


conditional value of information: the gain from learning that is available only if the irreversible action has not yet been
taken. The direct policy implication, developed further by Gollier et al. (2000) as an economic interpretation of the
precautionary principle, is that under uncertainty about consequences, irreversibility creates a systematic bias toward
caution that decision-makers must incorporate. This is the logic that the present framework operationalizes: when an
AI incident’s full consequences are uncertain at the point of triage, and the harm may be irreversible at one or more
levels, the framework defaults to provisional high severity, and this encodes the quasi-option value of not prematurely
downgrading an incident whose irreversibility has not yet been ruled out.
Operational frameworks in other, more mature, governance domains provide the second foundation. Financial regulation
under DORA (Articles 11–12) mandates that entities set, test, and maintain Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and
Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) for critical ICT systems, operationalizing recovery as a measurable, testable property
with well-defined temporal thresholds (European Commission, 2024). The cybersecurity domain under NIS2 (Article
21) treats system and data recoverability as a mandatory operational capability (European Parliament and Council
of the European Union, 2022b). The WHO rapid risk assessment framework assesses irreversibility at the level of
harm to the affected entity rather than at the level of system restoration, because in health the system and the harmed
entity are the same, i.e. the patient (World Health Organization, 2012). These frameworks share a common structure
of sequential recovery phases but each operates at the level of the entity experiencing the incident, not at the level of
downstream consequences. For example a financial regulator wants to know whether or not the bank can restore its
systems back to their previous capacity and capability, not whether any market distortions have been corrected. This
entity-level framing is not adequate for AI incidents whose consequences have the potential to propagate far beyond the
system that produced them. The framework therefore adopts a four-layer sequential assessment in which each layer is a
precondition for the next, each operates on a characteristic timescale, and each maps onto established analogues in
existing governance domains:

But the formal structure—a bounded continuous variable that can be assessed independently across dimensions of

a quantifiable input for triage decisions. In practice, the full value of D at each layer is rarely known at the point of

the quasi-option value principle: initial classification should reflect the upper bound of irreversibility consistent with
available evidence, because premature downgrading forecloses response options that cannot be recovered if the true D
turns out to be higher than initially estimated.
The sequential structuring is more than an organizational framing, it encodes a conditional logic for the assessment
of an incident’s recoverability: Containment (L1) is a precondition for meaningful control assessment (L2), because
control cannot be evaluated while the incident is still actively propagating. Control (L2) is a precondition for technical
restoration (L3), because you cannot restore a system you cannot direct. Technical restoration (L3) is a precondition
for societal restoration (L4), because societal recovery depends on the technical system functioning as intended. This
sequencing also implies increasing timescale and decreasing certainty in the initial assessment: L1 is assessable in
hours, L2 in days to weeks, L3 in weeks to months, and L4 may not be assessable for years. The framework addresses
this by requiring worst-case provisional estimates at an incident’s outset, this is then revised as information becomes
available and so it implements the Arrow-Fisher insight that under uncertainty and irreversibility the value of waiting
for better information before committing to a low-severity classification is strictly positive.
The Russian state-sponsored disinformation ecosystem documented in the AIID (Incidents 727, 884, 929, 968) illustrates
both the four-layer structure and the target-state problem. The Pravda network and its predecessor infrastructure have
flooded the internet with approximately 3.6 million articles per year, and a 2025 audit found that major AI chatbots
repeated Pravda-sourced narratives as fact with alarming frequency. At Layer 1, containment is partially achievable:
individual data sources can be blocked but new ones can be generated. At Layer 2, control cannot be fully restored:
no single entity controls all affected training pipelines across the multiple foundation model providers whose systems
have ingested the poisoned content. At Layer 3, technical state restoration would require coordinated retraining of
affected LLMs across the industry. This would be a cost and coordination challenge that renders full restoration
effectively irreversible. At Layer 4, the societal state, such as public trust in AI-generated information, the integrity of
the informational environment, etc., is subject to ongoing degradation with no clear recovery pathway.
This case also motivates the target-state concept. When full reversal to the pre-incident state is technically possible
but practically infeasible, the framework establishes a “target state” at which the incident is considered remediated,
with D defined as the residual harm at that target state. This is an established practice in environmental remediation,
where regulatory frameworks distinguish between “greenfield” restoration (full return to pre-contamination state) and
“brownfield” standards (acceptable residual contamination levels calibrated to intended future use) (US Environmental
Protection Agency, 2004). The question for good governance practice is whether or not the residual D at the negotiated
target state has consequences that warrant international coordination. A jurisdiction may determine that its AI systems
can operate at an acceptable performance level despite residual training data contamination, while that contamination
may have downstream impacts on other jurisdictions’ informational environments that those jurisdictions cannot
independently assess or remedy. The cross-border irreversibility test here is whether the permanent damage in one
jurisdiction has consequences that extend beyond it by virtue of interconnection, dependency, or precedent.

Descriptions of criteria
Criterion 1: Was AI a causal factor?
Purpose
Criterion 1 functions as a gateway filter, establishing whether an AI system was a causal factor
in the incident before any further assessment is undertaken. Where AI involvement is confirmed
or where confidence in AI’s causal contribution is assessed as medium or high, the incident is
retained for evaluation against the remaining criteria. Where AI involvement cannot be
established and confidence is assessed as medium/high, the incident is excluded from the
escalation process. In cases where confidence is low and evidence remains incomplete or
contested, the incident is provisionally retained, with parallel confidence-building activities
initiated pending a final determination.
Questions
Q1. Was AI present in the causal chain?
(Yes / No)
Q2. What is the confidence in AI’s causal contribution?
High — known / observed
Medium — potential / likely
Low — unclear / disputed
Overall response:
Yes if Q1 = Yes, regardless of Q2 confidence level. If Q2 = Low, this is noted and
confidence-building activities are initiated in parallel.
If Q1 = No, with High / Medium confidence in Q2, overall response = No (Disregard). If Q2
confidence is Low, confidence-building activities are initiated to resolve the uncertainty before
proceeding.

severity.
If Q1 = Yes and Q2 = No (root cause match but no related incident within window): assess as
individual incident. Proceed to criterion 5a.
If Q1 = No: assess as individual incident. Proceed to criterion 5a.
Legislative
Approaches
EU AI Act: The EU AI Act’s systemic risk definition acknowledges propagation “at scale
across the value chain” and includes a requirement to include patterns detected during
post-market monitoring that are related to a serious incident but does not operationalize a
pattern-detection mechanism.
SB 53: SB 53’s framing around “a single incident” with no correlated-incident aggregation
provision represents a coverage gap for cumulative incident types.
Cross-Domain
Precedent
Finance: The DORA Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 requires financial entities to
aggregate related ICT incidents sharing the same root cause or occurring within a rolling
6-month window, assessing the aggregated impact against materiality thresholds rather than
each incident individually. The Basel II event taxonomy provides complementary guidance: loss
events with a common root cause may be aggregated as a single event, and “boundary events”
(losses classifiable under multiple event types) are assessed for systemic risk implications.
Cybersecurity: MITRE ATT&CK maps adversary tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs)
as campaign patterns rather than isolated events: a series of individually low-severity
observations (initial access, discovery, lateral movement) constitutes a high-severity campaign
pattern when assessed collectively, with MITRE ATLAS extending this approach to AI-specific
attack chains (MITRE, n.d.b,n).
Challenges /
Limitations
Tracking prerequisites. Identifying patterns relating to a serious incident being assessed
requires tracking and analytics of incidents to be done and for clustering patterns to have been
defined.
Monitoring level. The level at which monitoring is done has implications for the incident
patterns which can be identified within and across AI model developers.
Cross-provider visibility. Pattern identification at the capability and contextual root cause
levels requires cross-provider incident visibility that is unlikely to be achievable by individual
providers acting alone. In practice, these checks can only be performed by a central
coordinating body with access to incident data across providers. Technical root cause matching
is the only level that a single provider can reliably perform at point of triage.
Taxonomy fragmentation. The use of different taxonomies and classification approaches
across providers and incident databases increases the difficulty of building a cross-provider
picture of systemic risk and incident patterns.
Centralized coordination. Clustering necessitates tracking and analytics of incidents: the level
at which monitoring is performed (individual provider vs. centrally coordinated) has direct
implications for which incident patterns can be identified.
34


Criterion 5a: Has harm occurred in a relevant category?
Purpose
Criterion 5a determines whether the harm falls within a recognized category before severity is
assessed. This step ensures the broadest possible range of AI-related harms is captured,
including harm types such as fundamental rights infringements, democratic norm violations, and
environmental damage that have no equivalent trigger under some existing frameworks, and that
novel incident types are not excluded simply because they were not pre-defined in regulation.
Questions
Q1. Has harm occurred within one or more of the categories in the MIT harm taxonomy?
Yes / No
Categories: physical harm, infrastructure damage, property damage, financial loss,
environmental damage, toxic or malicious content, differential treatment, human / civil rights,
democratic norms, and privacy.
Overall response:
If Q1 = Yes: proceed to criterion 5b for severity assessment in each identified harm category.
If Q1 = No: proceed to criterion 6 (the incident may still warrant escalation on the basis of
propagation dynamics, irreversibility, or near-miss status).
Legislative
Approaches
EU AI Act: The EU AI Act defines four broad serious incident categories
(Article 3(49)(a)–(d)): death or harm to health; disruption of critical infrastructure; infringement
of Union law obligations protecting fundamental rights; and harm to property or the
environment. These are assessed independently of the incident pathway: any AI system causing
harm in a qualifying category triggers the reporting obligation regardless of how the harm arose.
The Act’s category-based approach captures harm types, including fundamental rights
infringements and environmental harm, that have no equivalent trigger under SB 53.
SB 53: SB 53 does not define standalone harm categories. Instead, most critical safety incident
types combine a specified incident pathway with a specified harm outcome: weight exfiltration
resulting in death or bodily injury (§1107(d)(1)); materialisation of catastrophic risk
(§1107(d)(2)); loss of control causing death or bodily injury (§1107(d)(3)). The harm outcomes
recognized across these definitions are limited to death, bodily injury, and property damage — a
narrower set of categories than the EU AI Act’s four. This coupled structure also means that a
harm falling within a recognized category (e.g. bodily injury) would not qualify under SB 53
unless it arose through one of the specified pathways.
Cross-Domain
Precedent
Cybersecurity: NIS2 Article 6 defines harm to network and information systems across
availability, authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality, which constitute the harm domain for any
qualifying incident.
Finance: The Basel II Annex 2 operational risk event type categories classify financial losses
across seven event types (internal fraud, external fraud, employment practices, clients / products
/ business practices, damage to physical assets, business disruption and systems failures,
execution / delivery / process management), while DORA Article 18 defines major ICT-related
incident harm categories spanning availability of critical ICT services, data compromise,
regulatory obligation failures, financial losses above materiality thresholds, and reputational
impact.
Challenges /
Limitations
Abstraction mismatch. The GPAI Code of Practice Appendix 1.1 risk types (risks to public
health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society as a whole) and the Appendix 1.4
specified systemic risks (CBRN, loss of control, cyber offence, harmful manipulation) operate
at different levels of abstraction to the MIT harm taxonomy categories used at this criterion.
The CoP risk types describe domains of potential negative impact; the specified systemic risks
describe risk pathways or threat types through which a model might cause harm. SB 53 uses a
different abstraction again, generally defining each “critical safety incident” type as a risk
pathway combined with a harm outcome (see Appendix B). Neither maps one-to-one onto harm
categories, which complicates cross-framework comparisons and makes it difficult to verify
whether all escalation-relevant harms in one framework are captured by another.
Operational speed. The MIT harm taxonomy was designed for retrospective incident
classification, not real-time triage. Some categories (e.g. “democratic norms”, “differential
treatment”) may require investigation or contextual evidence that is unavailable at the point of
initial assessment, creating a tension between categorical completeness and operational speed.
Criterion 5b: Has harm crossed a relevant severity threshold?
35


Purpose
Criterion 5b determines whether the severity of harm identified at 5a warrants escalation. The
challenge is that existing frameworks use incompatible severity standards — from the EU AI
Act’s qualitative “serious” qualifier to SB 53’s quantitative thresholds of more than 50 deaths or
$1 billion in property damage — and a graduated scale is needed to capture incidents that fall
between these extremes.
Questions
Q1. Has harm in any single category reached Level 4 (Severe) or Level 5 (Catastrophic) on the
MIT severity scale?
Yes / No
The severity scale is a five-level scale applied per harm category, based on the CSET AI Harm
Framework with quantifiable criteria added by the MIT AI Risk Repository:
Level 1 — Negligible: minimal or no discernible impact
Level 2 — Minor: limited, easily remediated impact
Level 3 — Substantial: significant impact requiring intervention
Level 4 — Severe: serious, potentially lasting impact on individuals, organizations, or systems
Level 5 — Catastrophic: widespread, potentially irreversible harm including death, major
infrastructure failure, or large-scale societal disruption
Q2. Where harm has been assessed as a composite incident (criterion 4), is severity assessed
against the aggregated harm of the cluster?
Yes — severity assessment applies to the aggregated harm, not to each constituent incident
individually
Overall response:
If Q1 = Yes (Level 4 or 5 in any single harm category): Escalate.
If Q1 = No (all harm categories at Level 3 or below): proceed to criterion 6. The incident may
still warrant escalation on the basis of propagation dynamics, irreversibility, or near-miss status.
Legislative
Approaches
EU AI Act: The EU AI Act uses “serious” as the qualifying adjective for harm across most
categories but provides no explicit quantitative threshold beyond “death of a person”. For
fundamental rights (Art. 3(49)(c)), harm must rise to the level of an infringement of Union law
obligations, a legal standard rather than a quantitative threshold.
SB 53: SB 53 defines explicit quantitative thresholds: death or serious injury to more than 50
people, or more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to, or loss of, property arising from a single
incident involving a frontier model. For critical safety incidents under §1107(d)(1) and (d)(3),
the severity threshold is any death or bodily injury with no minimum count.
The result is that the EU AI Act’s qualitative “serious” standard provides interpretive flexibility
but limited operational specificity, while SB 53’s quantitative thresholds provide clear trigger
points but risk excluding incidents that fall just below the numerical minimums or that involve
harm types (such as rights violations or environmental damage) for which no quantitative
threshold is defined.
Cross-Domain
Precedent
Finance: The DORA Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772 classifies an ICT-related incident
as “major” if it affects a critical service and meets quantitative thresholds across multiple
dimensions: more than 10% of users or more than 100,000 clients impacted; duration exceeding
24 hours; the incident affecting two or more EU Member States; or financial impact exceeding
EUR 100,000.
AI Incident Databases: The MIT AIID Harm Taxonomy provides a five-level severity scale
(Catastrophic / Severe / Substantial / Minor / Negligible) applied per harm category by database
curators, while the OECD AIM proposes a three-tier classification ranging from “AI Incident”
(harm caused, typically limited in scope) through “Serious AI Incident” to “AI Disaster”
(large-scale, potentially irreversible harm causing widespread societal disruption).
Challenges /
Limitations
Legal operationalization. Many harm severities in the EU AI Act are defined using legal
terminology, such as “an infringement of Union law obligations” (EU AI Act Art. 3(49)(c)).
These are harder to operationalize as testable thresholds or trigger conditions, particularly under
time-sensitive escalation decision-making. However, relying solely on quantifiable thresholds
risks failing to escalate incidents that fall within the scope of legal repercussion.
Threshold gap. A gap exists between SB 53’s quantitative thresholds (death or serious injury to
more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage) and the lower boundary of
harm that may nonetheless warrant escalation. The death of a single person, serious injury to a
small number of individuals, or financial damage in the tens of thousands could each cross a
severity threshold depending on the domain, context, and affected population yet these fall far
below SB 53’s minimums and sit within the EU AI Act’s undefined “serious” qualifier.

Criterion 6: Is international coordination required to contain the incident or respond to its cross-border propagation?
Purpose
Criterion 6 determines whether an incident’s spread dynamics create an operational need for
international coordination — either to contain the incident, to warn exposed jurisdictions, or to
address capacity gaps that exceed national response.
Questions
Q1. Has confirmed harm occurred in two or more jurisdictions?
Yes / No
Q2. Is harm still propagating or accumulating at the time of assessment?
Yes / No
If Yes, classify the propagation pathway:
• Supply-chain propagation: shared infrastructure dependencies — how many downstream
systems or organizations inherit the failure mode because they rely on the same model,
component, provider, API, weights, dataset, or deployment pattern?
• Capability propagation: the harmful capability is reproducible or transferable — can the
failure mode be easily reproduced through fine-tuning, prompting, model transfer, open release,
copycat deployment, or user adaptation?
• Emergent propagation: harm spreads via AI interaction dynamics — does the harm amplify
through use dynamics rather than technical dependencies?
Q3. Does the propagation pathway cross national borders?
Assess using: downstream dependency count, jurisdictional spread, replicability / transferability,
and pathway determinism.
Yes / No
Q4. Does containment require action in another jurisdiction?
Yes / No
Q5. Is the propagating harm irreversible?
Yes / No
Q6. Is the affected jurisdiction’s response capacity sufficient?
Yes / No
Overall response:
If Q1 = Yes (confirmed cross-border harm): Escalate.
If Q1 = No but Q2 = Yes (active propagation): assess propagation pathway (Q3). If pathway
crosses borders and containment requires international action (Q4 = Yes): Escalate. If pathway
crosses borders but containment does not require international action: assess whether
propagating harm is irreversible (Q5). If Yes: Escalate. If No: Alert.
If Q2 = No (harm not propagating): proceed to criterion 7.
Legislative
Approaches
EU AI Act: While the EU AI Act recognizes propagation as a defining characteristic of
systemic risk (Article 3(65)), mandating that GPAI providers evaluate propagation pathways as
part of model-level risk assessment (Article 55, Annex XIII) and establishing cross-border
propagation of systemic risk as an explicit trigger for EU-level coordination (Article 66), these
obligations attach to models and providers, not to individual incidents. The Act does not specify
how propagation dynamics of a specific incident should be assessed or at what point
incident-level propagation should trigger escalation.
SB 53: Similarly, SB 53 does not address propagation as a standalone property of an incident
that could independently influence its classification. Propagation appears only implicitly
through loss-of-control provisions (§1107(c)(3)) and through the inclusion of cyberattack as a
catastrophic risk activity (§1107(c)(1)(B)). Neither provides for a sub-threshold incident to be
escalated on the basis of its propagation dynamics alone.
Cross-Domain
Precedent
Health: In epidemiology, Rc and doubling time function as real-time propagation metrics, and
the IHR Annex 2 embeds international spread risk as a criterion that triggers notification
regardless of current case severity.
Cybersecurity: Breakout time (CrowdStrike) sets the minimum detection window for
containment before propagation, MTTD / MTTR measure the interval between compromise and
response, and NIS2 Article 23(4) triggers cross-border notification when incidents affect two or
more EU member states.
Finance: DORA Article 19 triggers coordinated notification for major ICT-related incidents
affecting financial entities in multiple member states.
38


Challenges /
Limitations
1. Methodological gap. Existing AI governance frameworks do not account for incident-level
propagation assessment, meaning there is no established methodology for measuring
propagation dynamics of AI incidents in practice. The measurement techniques drawn from
comparator domains were each designed for specific, relatively narrow incident types within
well-characterized domains (biological transmission, network lateral movement, ICT service
disruption). How well these translate to the diversity of AI incident types, which span physical
harm, infrastructure disruption, informational harms, rights violations, and emergent behavioral
effects, is an open empirical question.
2. Infrastructure dependency. Effective incident-level propagation assessment, particularly
the cross-border scope question, depends on the ability to observe and correlate incidents across
providers, deployment contexts, and jurisdictions in a timely manner. This infrastructure does
not yet exist at the required scale. The propagation metrics drawn from comparator domains are
only feasible because of decades of investment in domain-specific surveillance and telemetry
networks.
3. Exposure estimation. For supply-chain propagation, exposure scope can often be estimated
by tracing the technical dependency tree (downstream integrations, API consumers, derivative
model deployments). For capability and emergent propagation, quantitative estimation of
exposure scope is substantially harder: the population at risk is defined by which models could
independently manifest the same behavior (capability) or which deployments share similar
interaction dynamics (emergent), neither of which is straightforwardly enumerable at the point
of assessment.
Criterion 7: Does irreversible harm require international coordination to assess or respond to its cross-border conse-
quences?
Purpose
Criterion 7 determines whether international escalation is warranted due to the consequences of
irreversible harm from a contained incident. It asks whether the permanent damage in one
jurisdiction has downstream effects on others — warranting international coordination not to
contain spread (assessed at criterion 6) but to assess and respond to permanent damage whose
consequences cross borders by virtue of interconnection, dependency, or precedent.
Questions
Q1. Is any portion of the harm irreversible?
Yes / No
Assess reversibility across four levels:
• Containment: Can further actions be halted before more harm propagates? Who has the
authority / responsibility to halt?
• Control restoration: Can the responsible actor regain the ability to direct, modify, or shut
down the system?
• Technical state restoration: Can the pre-incident technical state (model weights, training
data, system dynamics) be recovered?
• Structural and societal state restoration: Can the pre-incident infrastructure and societal
state be recovered? Highest level of irreversibility risk: macroeconomic / technical / societal
damage.
To estimate harm reversibility, look at cost / time / feasibility to reverse harm impacts assessed
in criterion 5. Any harm impacts which cannot be reversed are defined as D (change from
pre-incident state). Where full reversal is technically possible but at infeasible cost or timescale,
this is treated as effectively irreversible (drawing on the GPAI Code of Practice definition of loss
of control risk as situations where regaining control is “either extremely costly or impossible”).
Q2. Does the irreversible harm have consequences extending beyond the affected jurisdiction?
Yes / No
This is not asking whether the harm spread to other countries (assessed at criterion 6). It asks
whether the permanent damage in one jurisdiction has downstream effects on others, i.e. harm
crosses borders by virtue of interconnection, dependency, or precedent.
Overall response:
If Q1 = No (harm is fully reversible): proceed to criterion 8.
If Q1 = Yes and Q2 = Yes (irreversible harm with cross-border consequences): Escalate.
If Q1 = Yes and Q2 = No (irreversible harm contained within one jurisdiction): proceed to
criterion 8.
39


Legislative
Approaches
EU AI Act: The EU AI Act and SB 53 converge in treating irreversibility as an implicit
property of certain harm types rather than as an independent assessment dimension applicable
across all harm categories. The EU AI Act is the most explicit: Article 3(49)(b) names
irreversibility as a qualifying criterion for critical infrastructure disruption, and the GPAI Code
of Practice makes it definitional for loss of control risk (situations where regaining control is
“either extremely costly or impossible”). An incident causing serious but sub-threshold
irreversible harm to fundamental rights, property, or the environment has no accelerated
pathway under the Act on the basis of its irreversibility alone.
SB 53: SB 53 does not explicitly mention reversibility: its threshold structure assumes that
harm type and magnitude are sufficient for classification, meaning an incident producing
moderate but permanently irreversible harm has no escalation pathway that a comparable
reversible incident would not also have. The closest SB 53 comes is the implicit irreversibility
embedded in its harm outcomes (death, bodily injury), but these are classified by their nature,
not by their recoverability.
Cross-Domain
Precedent
Finance: DORA Articles 11–12 mandate that financial entities set, test, and maintain Recovery
Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) for all critical ICT systems,
measuring whether the service can be restored, not whether downstream consequences on
clients or markets can be reversed.
Cybersecurity: NIS2 Article 21 treats recoverability of data and system state as a mandatory
operational capability for essential entities, also framed at the system level.
Health: The WHO rapid risk assessment guidance is the closest any comparator domain comes
to assessing irreversibility at the harm level rather than the system level, because in health the
“system” and the “harmed entity” are the same (the patient): irreversibility (death, disability)
functions as a severity modifier within existing scoring rather than as a freestanding escalation
criterion.
Challenges /
Limitations
Temporal uncertainty. Estimating D (the irreversible component of harm) at the point of
triage is inherently uncertain, particularly for harm types where permanence only becomes
apparent over time. Physical harms such as death are immediately classifiable as irreversible;
economic, democratic, and informational harms may take months or years to reveal whether the
pre-incident state is recoverable.
Feasibility judgment. The distinction between absolute and effective irreversibility (technically
impossible vs. infeasibly costly) introduces a judgment call that different assessors may resolve
differently, particularly at Level 4 (structural and societal state restoration) where “feasible cost”
is inherently political. A jurisdiction with extensive resources may judge societal restoration
feasible where a less-resourced jurisdiction would not.
Information asymmetry. The cross-border consequences test at Step 2 requires the assessing
jurisdiction to evaluate downstream effects on other countries’ systems and interests: an
assessment it may not have sufficient information to make reliably, particularly for complex
interdependencies.
Criterion 8: Has a near miss or hazard indicated that harm is inadequately mitigated?
Purpose
Criterion 8 captures events where harm was closely averted but the failure mode revealed by the
near miss may indicate inadequate controls across the wider system. Its value lies not in the
averted incident itself but in what it reveals about control adequacy in analogous systems
elsewhere.
Questions
Q1. Has there been a closely averted incident that, had it not been averted, would have met the
severity threshold at criterion 5b (Level 4 or 5 on the severity scale)?
Yes / No
Q2. Does the failure mode that was averted affect, or could it plausibly affect, AI systems
deployed by other developers or in other jurisdictions?
Yes / No
Overall response:
If Q1 = Yes and Q2 = Yes (high-severity near miss with cross-system relevance): Alert.
If Q1 = Yes and Q2 = No (high-severity near miss but failure mode is system-specific): Discard
from international escalation. May warrant developer-level or national-level follow-up.
If Q1 = No (averted incident would not have met severity threshold): Discard.
40


Legislative
Approaches
EU AI Act: The EU AI Act and SB 53 converge in that neither mandates standalone near-miss
or hazard reporting in their binding text. Both frameworks are oriented primarily toward
incidents where harm has occurred or where a specified threatening condition has been
identified, rather than toward events where harm was plausibly close but averted. The EU AI
Act’s binding provisions (Article 73) activate only after a serious incident, with no provision for
near-miss events as independent reporting triggers. The GPAI Code of Practice introduces
near-miss obligations across several measures, but these are ancillary to other provider
processes (framework reassessment, systemic risk identification, model report updates, and
serious incident reporting) rather than constituting a standalone reporting channel, and the Code
is voluntary, not binding.
SB 53: SB 53’s §1107(d)(4) is an early warning trigger for a specified threatening capability
(deceptive techniques demonstrating materially increased catastrophic risk) rather than a near
miss in the sense of closely averted harm.
Cross-Domain
Precedent
Finance: The Basel II/III operational risk framework treats near-miss data as a relevant input to
operational risk management, feeding into scenario analysis and risk control self-assessments
rather than into the capital calculation framework directly.
Industrial Safety: The EU Seveso III Directive (2012/18/EU) requires operators of
establishments handling dangerous substances above specified thresholds to prepare Major
Accident Prevention Policies and implement Safety Management Systems: legally mandated,
comprehensive accident prevention strategies designed to prevent major accidents before they
occur, not merely to respond after harm materializes.
AI Incident Databases: The OECD AIM includes near misses within its definition of AI
hazards, and Longpre et al. (2024) propose a central reporting mechanism for “flaws” designed
to unify the possible security and safety implications of vulnerabilities and hazards.
Challenges /
Limitations
Scope limitation. Hazards corresponding to the risk pathways defined as immediate escalation
triggers (CBRN assistance, weight exfiltration, and loss of control) are already addressed at
criterion 3 regardless of whether harm has materialized. The scope of this criterion is therefore
limited to near misses outside those categories, which narrows its coverage but avoids
duplication.
Domain maturity. The comparator domains mandating proactive hazard reporting (Seveso III,
ICAO Annex 19, EU pharmacovigilance) do so within well-characterized domains with
operational maturity that AI governance does not yet possess. Replicating their hazard
assessment methodology, which requires assessing probability and pathway plausibility of
unrealized harm, raises distinct methodological challenges in the AI context.
Reporting gap. Near-miss data only reaches regulatory bodies as an ancillary obligation
attached to other reporting triggers: there is currently no independent requirement to report near
misses as standalone events under any binding AI governance framework.
Boundary classification. The boundary between a near miss and a low-severity incident is not
always clear-cut. An event where harm was averted by a functioning downstream control differs
from one where harm was averted by chance, and both differ from an event where minor harm
occurred but more severe harm was narrowly avoided. The framework does not yet specify how
to classify these boundary cases.

Testing: threshold walkthroughs with incidents
To stress-test our draft escalation criteria, we walked each threshold and trigger through a set of real AI incidents and
plausible variants, assessing how the framework classified them and where it broke down. Results of incident testing
are provided in Appendix E. The incidents tested were selected to cover a range of types, including the four high-risk
domains and novel domains, for example multi-agent and pathways involving model data poisoning, aimed to test edge
cases and surface learnings in those areas.
