5.2
Testing observations
The framework performed reliably for discrete-onset, individually severe incidents in which AI’s causal role is
identifiable within a specific event chain. The state-sponsored cyber attack (Incident 1) triggered a red line under SB 53,
and the data poisoning cluster (Incidents 9–10) escalated through the combination of pattern detection, cross-border
propagation, and irreversibility. For these incident types, causal confidence is typically high or medium because the
incident is bounded and the AI system’s involvement can be traced through documented evidence.
The framework was more challenged by three categories of incident, each of which reveals a distinct structural limitation:
• Cumulative, individually sub-threshold harms. For AI-related psychological harm (Incident 4) and cumulative
deepfake harms (Incident 2), the counterfactual test at the core of the causal chain criterion—‘would this harm
have occurred but for the AI?’—becomes essentially unanswerable at the individual interaction level, because AI
is one contributing factor among many across thousands of independent interactions. The testing suggests that
aggregation-based approaches to causality, such as demonstrating that a particular interaction pattern systematically
42


produces harm at rates differing from baseline, are needed as a supplement to individual counterfactual assessment.
Importantly, the framework’s multi-criteria architecture proved its value here: the cumulative deepfake incident
(Incident 2) did not trigger the red line gate (C3), which is designed for a different class of incident, but was correctly
caught at the harm severity gate (C5b) when assessed on an aggregate basis. This demonstrates that the sequential
design functions as intended, with downstream criteria compensating for upstream gates that are not engaged.
• Near-miss and potential harm. The agentic platform vulnerability (Incident 3) and the CBRN near-miss (Incident 6)
both expose a structural tension in the harm severity criterion: the MIT harm taxonomy assesses realized harm, but
these incidents’ significance lies almost entirely in their potential harm. For Incident 3, responsible disclosure by
security researchers contained the exposure within hours, producing low realized harm (severity 2–3) despite the
potential for severity 4–5 across financial loss, privacy, and infrastructure categories if the vulnerability had been
exploited maliciously. The near-miss criterion (C8) proved to be the strongest-performing criterion for these incident
types, correctly identifying the systemic risk signal. A design question remains as to whether responsible disclosure
should attenuate the urgency of the response pathway without attenuating the classification of systemic risk.
• Out-of-scope high-severity incidents. The military AI incident (Incident 7) produced a discard for what would be the
highest-severity incident in the test set, with estimated severity 5 and multiple red line triggers if the scope exclusion
did not apply. While the exclusion is by design, the testing raised the question of whether the framework should
include a ‘refer out’ pathway for incidents that fall within the military or defense exclusion but meet high-severity
indicators, and whether military AI incidents should be recorded at minimum to support cross-boundary pattern
detection.
In addition to these, the following further observations were made:
• Data availability. Data gaps were identified across nearly all incidents tested. The most consistent gap was access to
data held by AI developers, including interaction logs, training data provenance, internal safety assessments, and
internal escalation records. This data is unlikely to be shared voluntarily with an incident registry in the absence of a
legal obligation to do so. The agentic platform vulnerability (Incident 3) highlighted an additional gap: the relevant
data was held by the agentic platform operator rather than an AI model developer in the traditional sense, suggesting
that the framework’s assumed categories of data holders may need to be broadened as agentic AI deployment scales.
• Harm severity scales and thresholds did not capture the principal harm types from incidents in the large-scale
manipulation and psychological harm domain. The harm severity criterion (C5b) produced significant ambiguity
when applied to both incidents tested in this domain (Incidents 2 and 4). Neither incident reached Level 4 (Severe)
in any single harm category when assessed against the quantified scale descriptors, despite both producing harm
that regulatory and public responses clearly treated as severe. The MIT severity scale’s quantified thresholds for
Level 4 are calibrated to tangible outcomes(Slattery et al., 2025) but the principal harms in this domain, for example,
psychological distress, emotional dependence, dignity violation, and in severe cases self-harm or suicidal ideation, do
not map onto any of these descriptors. Both incidents scored Level 3 across multiple categories simultaneously, but the
per-category design provides no mechanism for cross-category aggregation. Additionally, the severity assessment for
the deepfake incident (Incident 2) was not modified by the involvement of children among the victims: AI Forensics
(AI Forensics, 2026) found nearly 10% of recovered content depicted minors in sexual activities, yet because the
scale contains no vulnerability modifier, the harm to child victims was assessed at the same severity level as the
harm to adults, despite the distinct legal treatment of such content under CSAM statutes across jurisdictions. For
both incidents, the cross-border nature of the propagation path caused these to escalate, rather than the severity
criterion. This means that for the large-scale manipulation and psychological harm risk domain, the severity criterion
is essentially non-functional.
• Lack of reliable evidence to confirm cross-border harm for incidents with diffuse detection channels. For
incidents in the large-scale manipulation and psychological harm domain, the evidence required to trigger cross-
border propagation checks at C6 is structurally difficult to assemble. The deepfake incident (Incident 2) had strong
cross-border evidence: regulatory investigations were opened in twelve named jurisdictions, providing concrete
documentation. The psychological harm incident (Incident 4) did not. OpenAI’s ~500k weekly affected users
figure is a global aggregate, not broken down by jurisdiction (OpenAI, 2025a). The specific confirmed harms: for
example lawsuits citing deaths by suicide (Social Media Victims Law Center, 2025), hospitalisations, and clinical
case reports, are concentrated in US reporting. The cross-border nature of the harm is inferred from the global
deployment of the models rather than documented from jurisdiction-specific harm reports. This evidentiary gap arises
because the detection channels for psychological harm—news reporting, litigation, social media discussion, and
clinical encounters—are fragmented and vary substantially in coverage across countries. The AI incident databases
(OECD AIM, AIID, MIT) that could in principle provide cross-jurisdictional evidence rely on English-language
media reporting, creating a systematic geographic bias. This means that for harm types where detection depends on
fragmented, media-dependent channels rather than systematic monitoring, the cross-border propagation criterion may
undercount the jurisdictions affected and underestimate the case for international coordination.
43


• The framework does not distinguish between ongoing background harm and acute escalation events. For
incidents where harm is cumulative and continuous rather than discrete, the framework’s propagation criterion
(C6) will always be satisfied once the harm is first detected: any globally deployed model producing ongoing
psychological harm has, by definition, an active propagation pathway that crosses borders. This creates a classification
problem. Psychological harm from human–AI interaction is not a discrete event with a beginning and an end—it is a
standing condition. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have published data indicating this is ongoing: OpenAI reported
that approximately 0.07% of weekly ChatGPT users exhibit risk factors including psychosis, mania, and suicidal
ideation (OpenAI, 2025a); Anthropic’s analysis of 1.5 million Claude conversations found disempowerment potential,
including reality distortion, value judgment distortion, or action distortion, in fewer than 1 in 1,000 interactions for
severe forms, with mild forms occurring in 1 in 50 to 1 in 70 conversations (Sharma et al., 2026). These figures imply
that developers currently treat these rates as falling within acceptable operating parameters. Once an ongoing harm of
this type has been identified for the first time, the operationally useful escalation trigger is not the continuing existence
of the harm but a spike in its prevalence or severity, analogous to how financial services regulators monitor fraud
losses against established baselines and escalate when losses exceed defined tolerances (European Commission, 2024).
An incident escalation framework should define thresholds for what constitutes an abnormal increase in an ongoing
cumulative harm, rather than treating the standing condition itself as a perpetual escalation trigger. Without such
thresholds, the risk is either that the ongoing harm is permanently escalated (rendering the escalation meaningless)
or that it is normalized (rendering the framework blind to deterioration). The current absence of agreed tolerances
also means that individual developers are implicitly setting their own baselines, creating the potential for divergence
between providers on what level of ongoing psychological harm is acceptable, compounding the challenges arising
from divergent harm definitions discussed earlier.
6
Discussion
Applying the framework to real incidents and structured variants, and analyzing existing AI incident frameworks against
them, surfaced ten findings about where escalation criteria work, where they break down, and what is required to
make them operational. A central finding was that escalation rules are only one part of the overall framework. Their
development and use depend on prior definitions of incident types, harm categories, severity scales, and principles for
grouping related incidents, as well as on the availability of relevant data to those responsible for assessing whether a
trigger condition has been met.
We group our findings (identified by F1) by where in this dependency chain they land (Figure 4). F1 concerns the
dependency structure itself. F2 and F3 concern the design of thresholds and triggers directly. F4, F5, and F6 concern
definitional foundations, including how harm is categorized, scored, and adjusted for affected populations. F7 and F8
concern clustering and aggregation methods: what constitutes a reportable incident and how related incidents are linked.
F9 and F10 concern the data architecture needed to operate the framework.

The dependency structure
Finding 1: Triggers and thresholds for AI incident escalation depend on definitional and data infrastructure
that does not yet exist.
The stress testing revealed that triggers and thresholds in the escalation layer cannot be
designed or operated without two other layers being in place. It relies upstream on definitional work specifying what
constitutes an incident, how harm is categorized and scored, and what unit of analysis applies (acute event, pattern, or
standing condition). It depends downstream on data infrastructure determining what can actually be detected: developer
telemetry, cross-developer pattern visibility, and cross-domain intelligence. The findings that follow (F2–F9) identify
specific gaps at each layer.
We present the dependency structure itself as a finding, because it provides an explanation for threshold design choices
in existing frameworks that risk systematic under-detection of incidents in certain systemic risk domains.
When the definitional layer is incomplete, threshold and trigger design is directly constrained. Triggers can only test
for conditions that have been defined in assessable terms; where harm categories are unspecified or specified in terms
that are not measurable against available data, triggers cannot be calibrated against them. Similarly, a defined unit of
analysis, whether the framework is assessing a single event, a cluster of related events, or an ongoing condition, is
a precondition for trigger design, because the trigger mechanism must be specified against whatever the framework
treats as a reportable incident. The effect is that threshold design defaults to harm types and incident structures for
which definitions already exist, leaving risk domains where they do not, particularly large-scale manipulation and
psychological harm, structurally harder to detect and escalate.
Recommendation (for policymakers and framework designers).
Design and assess AI incident escalation frame-
works against the full dependency chain, not only the escalation layer. Where definitional foundations are incomplete,
frameworks should specify interim triggers based on the information developers can observe (model behavior, inter-
action patterns, system states) rather than defaulting exclusively to confirmed harm outcomes that developers cannot
see. Investment in upstream definitional work—agreed harm categories, measurable severity scales, specified units
of analysis—is a precondition for operational triggers, rather than an optional refinement. The sequencing matters:
building triggers before the definitions and data layers are in place produces frameworks that are formally complete but
operationally unimplementable.
Thresholds and triggers
Finding 2: Some systemic risks warrant escalation before harm is confirmed, but current regulatory triggers
require confirmed harm outcomes.
Existing regulatory triggers (SB 53’s critical safety incident, the EU AI Act’s
serious incident definition) require harm outcomes such as death or property damage before reporting is activated in
most cases for incidents to be escalated. In these cases, the developer may see the triggering event but have no visibility
of downstream harm. The Tumbler Ridge shooting illustrated this: OpenAI closed an account for violent activity but
did not alert law enforcement because internal thresholds for credible, imminent risk were not met; the individual
subsequently committed a mass shooting (OpenAI, 2026b).
We identify three conditions that together justify immediate escalation without confirmed harm: the intervention window
is narrow; the probability of severe, irreversible harm without action is high; and no single actor has visibility over both
the risk pathway and the harm occurring.
Recommendation.
Define immediate-escalation triggers for systemic risks that have begun to materialize. Qualifying
events should include expert-level CBRN assistance; exfiltration of frontier model weights where containment is
unconfirmed; and AI systems or agent networks evading developer control. SB 53 partially addresses this for deceptive
subversion and the EU AI Act covers fundamental rights infringements, but weight exfiltration under SB 53 still requires
downstream harm outcomes the developer may never observe. The GPAI Code of Practice’s systemic risk identification
provisions could support detection but do not currently feed notification requirements.
Finding 3: Existing frameworks under-classify incidents presenting as patterns rather than discrete events.
The Grok deepfake incident (AI Incident Database, 2026) illustrated the gap: each individual image might score
severity 2–3, but millions of images, overwhelmingly targeting women, across a platform with hundreds of millions
of users reaches severity 4–5 in aggregate. A framework assessing only individual severity would classify this for
monitoring, not escalation. The same applies to human–AI interaction harms where individual harm is sub-threshold
but population-level effects are significant. Developers monitor relevant patterns: OpenAI on psychosis, self-harm,
and emotional reliance (OpenAI, 2025a); Anthropic on disempowerment patterns covering reality and value judgment
distortion (Sharma et al., 2026), but there is no agreed method for clustering, no consensus on aggregated thresholds,
and no obligation to report patterns as such.
46


Recommendation.
Define principles for grouping incidents for aggregated assessment. We propose three initial
groupings:
• Technical — shared root cause (same model, API layer, training dataset, upstream component).
• Capability — same behavior arising independently across models (sycophancy, hallucination-driven harm, persuasive
targeting).
• Contextual — same deployment pattern or affected population (companion chatbot dynamics, autonomous agent
tool-use patterns).
The Code of Practice’s post-market monitoring provisions (Measure 3.5) provide an aggregation mechanism but no
triggers or thresholds. This is particularly urgent for human–AI interaction harms, where consensus on categorising
concerning interaction patterns is itself a precondition for meaningful monitoring.
Definitional foundations
Finding 4: Some EU AI Act serious incident definitions are not specified in terms that support operational
detection.
Legal definitions are framed for regulatory and judicial contexts, not real-time escalation. Article 3(49)(c),
“infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights”, requires, before it can function as
a trigger, a mapping of all relevant obligations, a determination of what constitutes infringement of each, and translation
into indicators observable in developer data or incident databases. Article 3(49)(a), “serious harm to a person’s health”,
presupposes a measurable seriousness threshold, but none exists for developers with no visibility of downstream health
outcomes (see F1). Developers either set divergent internal thresholds or wait for confirmed harm that arrives too late
for meaningful intervention.
Recommendation.
Translate legally defined harm categories into measurable proxies that can be operationalized
before incidents occur. This requires dialogue between those drafting legal frameworks and those operationalizing them,
producing harm definitions that are both legally grounded and specified in terms of monitorable indicators. Proxies
should be established in advance, not derived ad hoc under time pressure. Tabletop walkthroughs of real incident types,
as used in this research, can surface definitions that appear clear in the abstract but prove difficult to apply in practice,
and should form part of the process by which legal definitions are stress-tested for operational use.
Finding 5: Harm severity scales are underdeveloped for large-scale manipulation and psychological harm,
leaving escalation thresholds underspecified.
Stress testing applied escalation criteria to two incidents in this
domain: mass non-consensual deepfake generation (Incident 2) and cumulative psychological harm from human–AI
interaction (Incident 4). Both produced documented real-world harm, with regulatory investigations across twelve
jurisdictions, reported hospitalisations, and deaths, yet applying quantified severity thresholds produced significant
ambiguity in both cases.
The principal harms, such as psychological distress, emotional dependence, and distorted perceptions of reality, are
difficult to observe (no visibility of downstream psychological outcomes), difficult to quantify (no equivalent of a
casualty count or financial loss figure), and difficult to attribute (the individual-level counterfactual is frequently
unanswerable). Any severity assessment here is therefore an approximation derived from proxy indicators, for example
interaction pattern data, risk factor prevalence, and media-reported cases, and no existing framework guides what level
of approximated harm is equivalent to a given severity threshold.
Recommendation.
Develop operational severity criteria for this domain through dedicated, multi-stakeholder work.
This requires clinical and safeguarding input on the pathways through which AI-mediated manipulation produces
psychological harm and on clinically meaningful indicators at different severity levels; developer input on what is
feasible to measure reliably from interaction data; and policymaker input on how the resulting categories map to existing
legal obligations, particularly how “serious harm to a person’s health” under the EU AI Act should be interpreted for
psychological harm. The output should be consensus guidance analogous to the WHO’s clinical severity scales (World
Health Organization, 2012) or DORA’s ICT materiality thresholds (European Commission, 2024).
Finding 6: Harm to vulnerable groups is not reflected as a severity modifier in any existing escalation framework,
despite being recognized in law, safeguarding practice, and AI developers’ own product architectures.
Identical
content produces materially different harm depending on who is affected. A non-consensual deepfake of a child is
legally distinct from one of an adult. CSAM statutes impose strict liability regardless of intent or volume, and the
IWF reported over 8,000 cases of AI-generated CSAM in the first half of 2025 (Internet Watch Foundation, 2026). A
chatbot reinforcing delusional thinking in a user with pre-existing psychosis presents a qualitatively different risk from
the same interaction with a resilient adult. Public-facing individuals (teachers, politicians, healthcare workers) face
47


disproportionate downstream consequences from the same content. Yet the severity scales tested here, and thresholds
in both the EU AI Act and SB 53, assess harm by type and magnitude without adjusting for who is affected. This
is in contrast with the frameworks these mechanisms operationalize. The EU AI Act identifies children and persons
with disabilities as warranting differentiated treatment (Recital 70, Article 5). Child protection law imposes strict
liability for harms involving minors. Developers already operationalize the distinction: OpenAI’s Teen Safety Blueprint
(OpenAI, 2025b) and Child Safety Blueprint (OpenAI, 2026a) deploy age prediction and differentiated safeguards, and
over 560,000 weekly users are flagged as exhibiting signs of psychosis or mania (OpenAI, 2025a), highlighting that
account-level classification infrastructure already exists.
Recommendation (developers).
Apply severity modifiers where accounts are flagged as belonging to vulnerable
groups. Classifications already generated for safeguarding, such as age prediction, mental health risk indicators, and
emotional dependence flags, should feed into incident severity assessment, so that incidents affecting flagged accounts
are assessed at higher effective severity than the same incident affecting the general population.
Recommendation (framework designers).
Incorporate vulnerability as an explicit severity modifier in escalation
criteria, specifying which population characteristics warrant upward adjustment and how they interact with existing harm
category thresholds, drawing on child protection law, the EU AI Act’s vulnerability provisions, and the population-level
risk data developers are already collecting.
Finding 7: For systemic risks manifesting as ongoing, low-severity harms rather than acute events, what
constitutes a reportable incident is not yet defined.
Existing escalation frameworks, including EU AI Act Article 73,
SB 53 §1107, and the framework tested here, are architectured around discrete events. Some systemic risk types do
not follow this model. Psychological harm from human–AI interaction, cumulative manipulation through generated
content, and gradual erosion of information integrity through training data contamination are standing conditions:
ongoing, low-severity harms across large populations, with no discrete onset, no point of resolution, and no single
incident to isolate. OpenAI reports approximately 0.07% of weekly ChatGPT users (around 500,000 individuals) exhibit
risk factors for psychosis, mania, or suicidal ideation (OpenAI, 2025a); Anthropic’s analysis of 1.5 million Claude
conversations found severe disempowerment potential in fewer than 1 in 1,000 interactions, with mild forms in 1 in
50 to 1 in 70, and prevalence of moderate and severe cases increasing between late 2024 and late 2025 (Sharma et al.,
2026).
Stress-testing exposed a structural problem: when harm is continuous and globally distributed, propagation and cross-
border criteria risk being permanently satisfied. Treat this as a perpetual trigger and escalation becomes meaningless;
do not, and a priority risk type is invisible. Established domains address analogous problems through tolerance-based
monitoring. Financial services treat fraud losses, which are ongoing, low-severity, high-frequency, by monitoring
against baselines and escalating when losses exceed defined tolerances (volume over time, rate of change, deviation
from expected range) (European Banking Authority, 2021). The Bank of England’s operational resilience framework
requires firms to set impact tolerances for important business services, defining the point at which disruption becomes
intolerable (Prudential Regulation Authority, 2022). The useful trigger is not the presence of harm but an abnormal
change in its rate, severity, or distribution: a principle not yet incorporated into any AI framework.
Recommendation.
Operationalize tolerance-based monitoring for ongoing harm types in three sequential steps:
1. Standardize harm categorizations. OpenAI’s “risk factors for psychosis, mania, and suicidal ideation” and
Anthropic’s “disempowerment potential” describe overlapping but non-identical phenomena using different
terminology, thresholds, and methodologies. Without agreed definitions, provider data cannot be compared,
aggregated, or assessed against common thresholds. The analogous work is standardisation of operational risk
event categories under Basel II.
2. Operationalize monitoring. Current disclosures are point-in-time research snapshots, not continuous feeds
comparable to financial transaction monitoring. Translating them into operational monitoring requires decisions
on measurement frequency, indicator selection, sampling methodology, and reporting format, informed by
what is feasible to measure reliably from interaction data.
3. Set tolerances and escalation thresholds. With standardized categories and operational monitoring in place,
the framework can define reportable events: prevalence spikes above baseline, sustained increases over defined
windows, threshold crossings in specific harm categories or affected populations. Without this, developers
implicitly set their own baselines: OpenAI’s 0.07% (OpenAI, 2025a), Anthropic’s “fewer than 1 in 1,000”
(Sharma et al., 2026), producing divergence that compounds divergent definitions.
48


Until these steps are completed, ongoing harms remain structurally difficult to detect, compare across providers, or
escalate consistently.
Finding 8: Present and emerging multi-agent AI risks are under-scoped in current frameworks.
Four adjustments
are needed. First, the international regulatory net catches some AI incidents only by their downstream sectoral impact,
not their upstream causal structure, which may sit in a different jurisdiction from the reported incident. Second, a useful
unit of analysis is the joint hazard object: an AI system together with its deployment environment and the population of
agents (human and AI) it interacts with; propagation and coordination dynamics are properties of this joint object, not
of the model in isolation. Third, while academic attention focuses on emergent multi-agent dynamics as the frontier
risk, present-day threats concentrate in coordinated multi-agent systems, deliberately directed use of multiple agents
by upstream actors operating outside the jurisdictions where incidents are detected. Both require governance, but
coordination is where deliberate cross-border threats are already materializing and where the incident-report architecture
is weakest. Fourth, in AI-specific frameworks with well-defined triggers, multi-agent risks are largely absent from
trigger conditions themselves; where mentioned, provisions are typically voluntary, non-specific, and unattached to
thresholds or reporting obligations. Even when coordinated or emergent multi-agent harms fall within nominal scope,
no operational mechanism exists to classify, escalate, or coordinate response.
Recommendation.
Three targeted additions to existing instruments:
1. Trigger conditions: Multi-agent risk factors—interaction topology, joint hazard specification, orchestration
scope, cross-jurisdictional propagation—should be written into the trigger conditions of AI-specific frameworks
alongside existing single-system criteria.
2. Reporting obligations: Reporting should capture upstream causal or clustering structures and possible
orchestration indicators, not only downstream sectoral impact.
3. Coordination pathways: Coordination pathways should be pre-specified for incidents where the jurisdiction
of detection is not the jurisdiction of causation; the defining feature of the coordinated multi-agent threats
already materializing.
These additions are modest in instrument design but substantial in effect, converting incidental, downstream-only
visibility of multi-agent harms into a governed, upstream-aware regulatory architecture.
Data architecture
Finding 9: Data required to operate escalation triggers is dispersed across sources, most of which are not
currently accessible.
Scenario testing exposed that trigger-relevant data is distributed across sources with very
different accessibility and reliability. Public incident databases (AIID, AIAAIC, OECD AIM) are the most accessible
but rely on media reports, use incompatible schemas, lack consistent severity data, and cannot support real-time detection.
Individual developer data includes privileged technical knowledge on model behavior, model–user interactions, and
internal safety incidents, but remains proprietary and does not flow into public infrastructure. Even within a single
developer’s view, monitoring may not be structured to surface escalation-relevant patterns, and absent consensus on
what constitutes a concerning pattern, detection and aggregation approaches diverge across developers. Requiring
developers to assess likelihood of real-world harm from model behavior alone is a further constraint where they have
no visibility of downstream outcomes: a limitation acknowledged by Sharma et al. (2026), whose analysis captured
potential rather than confirmed harm. For pattern-based triggers such as shared failure modes, frequency acceleration,
geographic clustering, and multi-provider orchestration, a single developer’s view is structurally insufficient.
Recommendation (policymakers).
Map the data requirements for each escalation trigger, distinguishing those
assessable from a single developer’s data (harm severity within a known deployment, system-state reversibility after
technical failure) from those requiring a cross-developer view (shared failure modes, ecosystem-wide frequency
acceleration, geographic clustering, multi-provider orchestration). For each cross-developer trigger, specify what data
is needed, at what aggregation or granularity, for what analytical purpose, with what timeliness. Use this mapping to
design data-sharing arrangements, via a regulatory body, independent intermediary, or mutual reporting mechanism,
alongside convergence on shared harm-category definitions, classification schemas, and incident-grouping techniques.
Recommendation (developers).
Establish voluntary cross-developer mechanisms for incident visibility. Structured
sharing of aggregated signals, such as categories of incidents observed, frequency trends, and capability domains
implicated, through bodies such as the Frontier Model Forum need not require sharing proprietary model data or detailed
reports, and would provide a materially better basis for distinguishing local anomalies from ecosystem-wide shifts, as
49


well as identifying shared upstream causes (common training data issues, API-layer vulnerabilities) no single developer
can detect alone. Establishing these proactively rather than waiting for regulatory mandates would improve individual
risk management and demonstrate industry capacity for collective action.
Finding 10: The framework’s capacity-gap assessment at C6 cannot be operationalized without pre-established
national response capacity data that does not currently exist for AI incidents.
The framework’s propagation
assessment (Criterion 6, Step 5) asks whether the affected jurisdiction’s response capacity is sufficient, and classifies a
capacity or information gap as grounds for an international alert (Response Classification 4). This assessment cannot
be made at the point of incident triage unless the relevant information has been established in advance. Whether a
jurisdiction can detect, investigate, contain, and recover from an AI incident depends on characteristics not observable
from the incident itself: the maturity of domestic AI incident response institutions, the degree of AI integration in
critical national infrastructure, regulatory readiness to act on AI-specific incidents, and available technical workforce.
Without prior assessment, the capacity question in C6 is either unanswerable or answered informally and inconsistently.
Established frameworks address this through standing national capacity assessments that pre-date specific incidents.
Under the World Health Organization (2005), all 196 states parties are required to report the status of their surveillance
and response capacities annually to the World Health Assembly through the States Parties Self-Assessment Annual
Reporting tool (SPAR), which assesses 15 capacities using 35 indicators. The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk
Reduction (2015)Sendai Framework similarly requires countries to adopt national disaster risk reduction strategies
(Target E) and to self-report against defined indicators, incorporating capacity assessment as a standing dimension of
risk. In both cases, the assessment exists as a pre-established input to incident triage, not a determination made under
time pressure. No equivalent mechanism exists for AI incidents.
Recommendation.
Develop a standardized template for countries to characterize their AI incident response capacity
and risk surface in advance, as a standing input to the alert determination at C6. The template should cover dimensions
relevant to the capacity-gap assessment: AI integration in critical infrastructure, maturity of domestic incident response
institutions, regulatory readiness, and technical workforce. The WHO IHR SPAR (World Health Organization, n.d.)
provides a direct design precedent: a structured self-assessment instrument, reported on a regular cycle, producing a
comparable profile across countries. A similar instrument for AI could be self-declared, subject to peer review, and held
by the relevant reporting body.
6.1
Future research
Most of the research directions below extend specific findings in this paper and are indexed to the relevant finding in the
summary matrix above. Two items—empirical validation through tabletop exercises and mapping adjacent regulatory
coverage—represent priorities that go beyond the scope of the paper’s core findings.
Risk-domain-specific trigger refinement (F2).
Each risk domain (CBRN, cyber, human–AI interaction harms,
democratic process manipulation) has distinct characteristics that affect how triggers should be calibrated. Deep dives
into trigger design per risk domain are needed, with particular attention to domains where AI developers can only
identify hazards but not confirm real-world harm (CBRN, lethal autonomous weapons), and domains where harm
presents as patterns rather than discrete events. For CBRN, the stress testing (Incident 6) retrospectively validated
the design rationale for pre-harm escalation triggers: because AI’s causal contribution to CBRN events is difficult to
establish after the fact and the evidence is held by law enforcement and intelligence services rather than AI developers,
capability-based escalation before harm is confirmed is justified. Future work should explore whether graduated
evidentiary standards, specifying, for each risk domain, what level of approximated or proxy evidence is sufficient for
escalation, should replace the current uniform approach, calibrating the required confidence level to the reversibility
and propagation potential of the harm in question.
Data architecture for incident detection (F9).
The stress testing revealed two qualitatively distinct data gaps
requiring different solutions. The first is cross-developer data: pattern detection for incidents like cumulative deepfake
harms (Incident 2) and psychological harm (Incident 4) requires visibility across providers to identify shared capability
or contextual root causes. This is achievable through cross-developer data-sharing arrangements with appropriate
anonymisation and interoperability standards. The second is cross-domain intelligence: the GRU-linked incident cluster
(Incidents 9–10) was linked not through AI system telemetry but through national intelligence analysis (VIGINUM),
investigative journalism, and independent media auditing (NewsGuard). Even perfect cross-developer visibility would
not have detected this pattern, because three of the four incidents in the cluster produced no meaningful signal in any AI
developer’s systems. Future work should systematically evaluate which data elements are needed for each trigger type,
distinguishing between those that require cross-developer sharing (specifying aggregation levels, privacy-preserving
50


techniques, and interoperable schemas) and those that require cross-domain intelligence interfaces with institutions
whose mandates already encompass adversarial campaign detection.
Incident clustering and aggregation methods (F7, F8).
The stress testing revealed three specific limitations in the
current design. First, the rolling time windows (30/60/90 days) can expire before retrospective evidence links older
incidents: the GRU cluster was identified months or years after individual incidents occurred, and the framework has
no mechanism for re-opening expired windows when new evidence emerges. Second, the root cause categories are
system-oriented (shared model, shared behavior, shared deployment pattern) and do not capture actor-oriented linkages
(shared adversary), which are characteristic of coordinated campaigns. Third, for human–AI interaction harms where
individual incident severity is low but aggregate harm is significant, the clustering mechanism must work in conjunction
with severity scales that can assess composite harm; a dependency that is currently unsatisfied given the gaps in severity
calibration for this domain identified in this paper. Future work should provide guidance on how incidents should be
detected from monitoring requirements and would provide clarity to AI developers on what patterns to look for and
report.
Vulnerability-modified severity assessment (F6).
Vulnerability modifiers are recognized in law (CSAM statutes, EU
AI Act Recital 70 and Article 5) and increasingly in AI developers’ own product architectures. OpenAI has deployed age
prediction and differentiated safeguards for minors (OpenAI, 2026a) and has published data on users exhibiting mental
health risk indicators (OpenAI, 2025a). Future work should explore how account-level vulnerability classifications
already generated for safeguarding purposes (age prediction, mental health risk indicators, emotional dependence flags)
could be connected to incident severity assessment, and what governance framework would be needed to ensure such
modifiers are applied consistently across providers while protecting user privacy.
Tolerance-based escalation architecture for ongoing harms (F7).
A significant subset of AI systemic risk types—
psychological harm from human–AI interaction, cumulative manipulation, gradual information integrity erosion—
manifest as ongoing, low-severity, high-frequency harms rather than discrete events. The stress testing demonstrated
that the framework’s propagation criterion is permanently satisfied for these harm types once first detected, creating a
binary that is either meaninglessly perpetual or blind to deterioration. Future work should develop a tolerance-based
monitoring approach modeled on financial services, where reportable events are defined as deviations from agreed
baselines rather than the existence of harm per se (European Commission, 2024; Prudential Regulation Authority,
2022). This requires a sequenced programme: first, multi-stakeholder agreement on standardized harm categories;
second, operationalization of continuous monitoring by AI developers against those categories; and third, definition of
escalation tolerances specifying what magnitude of change over what time period constitutes an abnormal deterioration
warranting escalation.
Mental and psychological harm definition and severity calibration (F5).
Mental and psychological harm features
in the European Commission (2025) (Measure 9.3 explicitly references “serious harm to a person’s health (mental
and/or physical)”) but remains difficult to define in a measurable way. The problem is not only definitional but extends
to severity calibration, where no existing scale provides thresholds for psychological and dignitary harm types, and to
monitoring feasibility, where real-world outcomes (self-harm, hospitalisation, relationship breakdown) are not directly
observable by AI developers. Future work could seek to provide a working definition that could range from clinically
recognized and diagnosed harm, to dependency, reality distortion, or reliance on AI for decision-making, to confirmed
harm following reality distortion events. Building consensus requires input from clinical and safeguarding experts
on harm pathways and meaningful severity indicators, from AI developers on what proxy indicators can feasibly be
measured from interaction data, and from policymakers on how the resulting thresholds relate to legal obligations
including the interpretation of “serious harm to a person’s health” under the EU AI Act. Emerging understanding of
human–AI interactions, including OpenAI’s risk factor data (October 2025) and Anthropic’s disempowerment analysis
(Sharma et al., 2026), provides an empirical foundation on which this consensus work could build.
Multi-agent attribution frameworks (F8).
Further work is needed on how to assess causation and attribute harm
in multi-agent systems, including whether interactions between agents materially altered outcomes beyond what a
single-agent deployment would have produced. This should address the three distinct harm multiplication mechanisms
identified in this paper: shared-dependency failures that scale linearly, coordinated failures that concentrate attribution,
and emergent harms attributable only to the collective dynamic.
Empirical validation through tabletop exercises.
Applying the framework to real incidents and structured variants
with stakeholders, including policymakers, AI developers, and the public, to validate escalation decisions and refine
criteria in response to concrete cases. The process of walking through specific incidents provides an opportunity to
51


build a shared understanding of which incidents warrant escalation and why, and to adjust criteria where they produce
surprising or inappropriate outcomes.
Mapping adjacent regulatory coverage.
This work drew on a narrow set of AI-specific regulatory sources. Decisions
within the design of existing frameworks may have been influenced by adjacent regulation already covering provisions
for certain types of related incident (for example, the Digital Services Act). Mapping related and sector-specific
escalation requirements to identify specific gaps for AI risk types and to avoid duplicating provisions that already exist
elsewhere would strengthen the framework’s positioning within the broader regulatory landscape.
7
Conclusion
Our work highlights how the design of AI incident escalation frameworks, including the criteria assessed, the order
of assessments, the thresholds and triggers, directly determines which incidents will be detected and escalated. If the
purpose of an escalation framework is to enable early detection of real-world incidents, its design must account for the
pathways by which different risks materialize, who can observe each step, what data is available at each point, and the
specific limitations that apply. Failing to do so risks producing a framework that is fundamentally unimplementable
under real-world constraints.
In domains where risk pathways are less well understood, particularly manipulation and psychological harm, and
loss-of-control risks, significant gaps remain: in what constitutes an incident, in how to treat single versus clustered
events, and in how to define severity and harm type. This is a more fundamental challenge, because the definitional
building blocks required to design detection and monitoring patterns are themselves missing. Point-in-time reports on
these incident types advance our understanding, but building ongoing monitoring without clarity at the definitions layer
risks creating divergence across developers, making cross-developer risk trend analysis harder over time.
Finally, the data required to identify incidents is distributed across public AI incident databases, AI developers, and
third-party organizations including law enforcement, security services, and other incident-reporting domains. To
understand the practical impact of these data gaps and prioritize efforts to surface and combine data, mapping exercises
are needed, tracing the data elements required for detection and evaluation across primary risk domains, identifying
which data matters most, who holds it, and what is required to access it, so that the data needed to detect and escalate
the most severe incidents is available in practice.

Additional clarification of regulatory requirements
This appendix provides supplementary detail on regulatory provisions referenced in Section 2.1. The material below is
drawn from the same primary sources cited in the main text and is included here to support readers requiring the full

A.1
EUAIA high-risk system domains, risk management, and prohibited practices
A.1.1
High-risk system domains and risk management
Such systems are listed in Annex III, including systems used in biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and
vocational training, employment, access to essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration and border
control, and the administration of justice and democratic processes. For such systems, Article 9 requires a continuous
iterative risk-management process, including evaluation of other risks arising on the basis of data gathered through
post-market monitoring (Art. 9(2)(c)) (European Parliament and Council, 2024).
A.1.2
Prohibited practices (Article 5)
The prohibited practices listed in the EUAIA are extensive. These include systems causing discriminatory impacts
and unfair bias prohibited under Union or national law (Recital 27); manipulative, exploitative, and social control
practices (Recital 28); AI-enabled manipulative techniques that materially distort human behavior in ways likely to cause
sufficiently important adverse impacts on physical or psychological health or financial interests, including by exploiting
vulnerabilities or impairing autonomy, decision-making, or free choice (Recital 29); and biometric categorization
systems used to infer political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, race, sex life, or
sexual orientation, subject to limited carve-outs (Recital 30) (European Parliament and Council, 2024).
The Act also prohibits social scoring of natural persons (Recital 31), certain forms of real-time remote biometric
identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (Recitals 32–33), judgments about persons
based solely on predicted behavior derived from profiling or personality traits without reasonable suspicion of criminal
activity (Recital 42), systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial
images (Recital 43), and systems inferring emotions or intentions in work or education contexts on the basis of biometric
data (Recital 44). These practices are also reflected in Article 5.
A.2
DSA provisions: data access, crisis protocols, and crisis-response powers
Additional DSA provisions aimed at preventing ‘dark patterns’ may also help mitigate manipulation, psychological
harm, and risks to democratic integrity. Article 35(1)(h) signals that where risks are shared across platforms, providers
should cooperate, implicitly recognizing that cross-platform aggregation is relevant to systemic risk identification.
However, this is a soft expectation rather than an enforceable requirement.
Article 48 of the DSA also outlines voluntary crisis protocols for ‘crisis situations’ or ‘specific extraordinary cir-
cumstances’. Yet the Commission has not fully specified the parameters for determining what constitutes such a
circumstance. This contributes to a pattern of incomplete soft enforcement, mirrored in the voluntary nature of the
General-Purpose AI Code of Practice and the absence of further detailed guidance in some areas of implementation.
A.2.1
Article 40: researcher data access
The DSA makes a further contribution through Article 40, which creates a legally grounded data access mechanism
enabling researchers to request data from VLOPs and VLOSEs for the purpose of detecting, identifying, and under-
standing systemic risks in the Union. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/2050 operationalizes this through
the DSA Data Access Portal. The mechanism operates across two tiers: Article 40(4) grants vetted researchers access
to non-public platform data, but requires affiliation with a research institution; Article 40(12) provides a broader access
route to publicly available data for researchers affiliated with not-for-profit bodies, organizations, and associations,
without the institutional affiliation requirement. Article 40 may therefore help support cross-platform pattern analysis
of manipulation, disinformation, and psychological harm incidents—precisely the risk categories where an aggregated
view across actors is most needed and where single-provider reporting is structurally insufficient.
However, three limitations constrain this mechanism’s utility. The first is jurisdictional: Article 40 applies to VLOPs
and VLOSEs and not to AI model providers. The second is operational: enforcement of Article 40 has been actively
contested, with formal proceedings opened against X and Meta, among others, for failures to comply. Article 40 is also
researcher-initiated and application-dependent: it creates a right of access rather than a standing monitoring function,
59


thereby generating episodic research outputs rather than the continuous cross-developer pattern detection that effective
systemic risk monitoring requires.
A.2.2
Article 36: crisis-response mechanism
Article 36 of the DSA establishes a crisis-response mechanism enabling the Commission to require specific mitigation
measures from VLOPs and VLOSEs where a ‘serious threat to public security or public health’ has arisen (Art. 36(2))
(European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022c). This is a propagation-aware emergency provision in
the sense that it is designed for situations where harm is spreading faster than routine regulatory response can address.
However, Article 36 is reactive and Commission-initiated—it responds to crises in progress, rather than enabling pre-
emptive escalation when propagation indicators are detected early. Article 36(1)(c) ambiguously states that providers
must report to the Commission ‘by a certain date or at regular intervals’ without giving additional detail beyond that
providers must ‘take due account of the gravity of the serious threat’ (Art. 36(3)(a)) and that the specific measures
taken are to be ‘limited to a period not exceeding three months’ (Art. 36(3)(c)), which may be further extended
(Art. 36(8)(b)). Critically, Article 36 has not been enforced to date, meaning its practical utility as a propagation-based
trigger remains untested. In cases where the propagated harm involves poisoned data, the data quality failures identified
under Articles 10 and 15 (AIA), which concern data governance and accuracy, currently involve no escalation triggers
for when such poisoned data is detected, because it is classified as an ‘AI specific vulnerability’ (Art. 15(5) AIA) rather
than as a serious incident.
A.3
Code of Practice reporting mechanics (Measures 9.1–9.3)
A.3.1
Methods for serious incident identification (Measures 9.1–9.2)
Methods for serious incident identification under Measure 9.1 include reviewing external sources of information, such
as police and media reports, research papers, and incident databases, and facilitating reporting by downstream modifiers,
downstream providers, users, and other third parties (European Commission, 2025).
Measure 9.2 further recommends reporting on the start and end dates of the incident, the resulting harm and affected
group, the chain of events leading to the serious incident, root-cause analysis, and patterns detected during post-market
monitoring, including near misses.
A.3.2
Reporting timelines (Measure 9.3)
Reporting timelines under Measure 9.3 of the Code of Practice are not faster than those under Article 73 of the EUAIA,
with the exception that serious cybersecurity breaches, including model-weight exfiltration and cyberattacks, where
signatories establish or suspect with ‘reasonable likelihood’ a causal relationship between their model and the breach,
are to be reported within five days (Measure 9.3(2)) (European Commission, 2025).
A.4
SB 53: OES reporting mechanism and frontier framework requirements
Section 1(m) calls for the timely reporting of critical safety incidents to government. Most notably, Chapter 25.1,
§22757.12(a), in force from 1 January 2026, requires large frontier developers to publish a frontier framework
describing their approach to incorporating standards and best practices, defining and assessing catastrophic-risk
thresholds, revisiting and updating the framework, identifying and responding to critical safety incidents, and assessing
and managing catastrophic risk arising from the internal use of frontier models (California State Legislature, 2025b).
SB 53 assigns the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (OES) a role in receiving reports of AI incidents
that meet catastrophic-risk thresholds. Under §22757.13(a), the OES must establish a reporting mechanism that can be
used by frontier developers or members of the public to report a critical safety incident. Under §22757.13(c), frontier
developers must report critical safety incidents relating to one or more frontier models within 15 days of discovery,
disclose within 24 hours where a critical safety incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury to an
appropriate law-enforcement or public-safety agency, file amended reports where relevant, and are encouraged, but not
required, to report critical safety incidents relating to foundation models (California State Legislature, 2025b).
Large frontier developers must also transmit to the OES a summary of any assessment of catastrophic risk resulting
from internal use of frontier models every three months, or on another ‘reasonable schedule’ specified by the developer.
Beginning 1 January 2027, the OES must produce an annual report containing anonymized and aggregated information
about critical safety incidents that have been reviewed.

Detailed comparative analysis of existing frameworks against our criteria
Incident escalation rapid assessment framework
This section presents eight assessment criteria for determining whether an AI incident warrants escalation, and defines
the thresholds and triggers associated with each. To inform the design of these criteria, we conducted a structured
comparative analysis across three source categories: AI-specific regulatory frameworks (the EU AI Act and California’s
SB 53), classification approaches used by major AI incident databases (OECD AIM, AIID, MIT), and established
incident management practices in analogous high-risk domains (health, finance, and cybersecurity). These sources
are not treated as models to be replicated directly; AI incident escalation operates in a distinct context with its own
constraints, including attribution uncertainty, rapid capability change, and cross-border digital propagation, that no
existing domain fully addresses. Rather, each source provides design candidates: specific mechanisms, threshold
structures, and classification logics that have been tested operationally in mature governance regimes and that may be
adapted to the AI incident context. For each criterion, we present the most relevant precedents from regulation, incident

results. This illustrates how disallowed practices can be defined in absolute, without linking harm assessment of these. However, the serious incidents themselves are defined in

F
Topological structure of multi-agent AI propagation dynamics
F.1
Purpose and scope
The main text identifies the propagation mechanisms — common exposure, environmental coupling, network contagion,
and their compounding through interdependence — that determine how AI incidents escalate. This appendix provides
the formal topology-specific treatment: how the T0–T3 classification (defined below) maps onto distinct propagation
regimes, what structural features of the deployment environment determine the propagation profile within each regime,
and how transitions between regimes can be detected through information-theoretic measurement.
The classification is structured as follows. Section F.2 introduces the topological framework and defines the four
categories. Section F.3 specifies the propagation profile for each category. Section F.4 formalizes how the five
environmental structure dimensions shape propagation within and across categories. Section F.5 details the T1→T3
transition mechanism (signal endogenization) as a change in the effective propagation structure. Section F.6 defines the
information-theoretic measurement signatures that distinguish topology categories and detect transitions between them.
Section F.7 addresses the operationalization of these signatures as calibrated escalation triggers.
F.2
The topological risk framework (T0–T3)
The topological risk framework classifies multi-agent AI configurations according to the source of behavioral corre-
lation3 between agents. The question we address is this: when multiple AI agents exhibit correlated behavior, what
is the causal mechanism producing that correlation? The answer determines the propagation profile, the appropriate
governance response, and the conditions under which international coordination becomes necessary.
The framework defines four categories:
T0: Independent deployment. Each agent operates independently. There is no mechanism, either exogenous or en-
dogenous, producing behavioral correlation between agents. Agents are functionally, behaviorally, and mechanistically
isolated from each other: no shared real-time inputs, no observation of each other’s outputs, no interaction through a
shared environment. Aggregate harm scales linearly with the number of deployments: f(N) = N. T0 is below the
multi-agent threshold; it is included as the baseline against which multi-agent dynamics are defined. We note that AI
capability is often measured on the assumption that all AI deployments are isolated in this sense.
T1: Common-cause correlation. Agents exhibit correlated behavior because they share an upstream dependency:
common training data, a shared foundation model, shared infrastructure, or a common exogenous signal (e.g. a market
price feed). The correlation is exogenous — it originates outside the agent interaction and would persist even if agents
could not observe each other. Removing the shared upstream source eliminates the correlation. T1 is the regime of
correlated failure without contagion: agents fail simultaneously because they share a vulnerability, not because one
agent’s failure triggers another’s.
T2: Hierarchical orchestration. A single orchestrating entity (which may itself be an AI system) directs multiple
sub-agents toward a coordinated objective. The correlation is deliberately imposed by the orchestrator rather than
arising from shared upstream causes or emergent dynamics. T2 is structurally orthogonal to the T1–T3 spectrum:
an orchestrated system can simultaneously exhibit T1 properties (sub-agents sharing common training data) or T3
properties (sub-agents developing emergent coordination beyond the orchestrator’s design). The orchestration hierarchy
is an additional structural layer that shapes propagation independently of the correlation source.
T3: Emergent interaction. Agents exhibit correlated behavior that is produced entirely by the interaction dynamics
between agents. There is no shared upstream cause driving the correlation and no orchestrator imposing it. The
coordination arises endogenously from the agents’ mutual observation of, and response to, each other’s behavior within
a shared environment. T3 is the regime of emergent equilibria: the correlated behavior is self-sustaining, and persists
even if the initial conditions that seeded it are removed. T3 dynamics can produce qualitatively new outcomes — phase
transitions, lock-in to harmful equilibria, collective behaviors not present in any individual agent’s design — that
represent the most challenging category for governance because the harm is a property of the interaction structure rather
than of any identifiable agent.
T3 is the most difficult topology category to build intuition for, as the harmful outcome is not attributable to any agent’s
design or intent. Microsoft’s Tay chatbot (2016) provides an early cautionary illustration (Neff and Nagy, 2016; Wolf

et al., 2017). Tay was a single AI agent with online learning deployed into a reactive environment (Twitter) where its

The resulting behavior was not designed by Microsoft, not achievable by any individual user, and not attributable to Tay’s

F.3
Propagation regimes by topology category
Each topology category exhibits a characteristic propagation profile: a combination of scaling behavior, cascade
mechanism, propagation speed determinant, and intervention architecture.
F.3.1
T0: Independent deployment
Propagation scaling. Linear: f(N) ≃N. Doubling the number of deployed agents doubles the aggregate harm. There
is no inter-agent propagation pathway; each agent’s contribution to harm is independent of all others.
Cascade mechanism. None. Failures are statistically independent. The failure of one agent provides no information
about the probability of failure in any other agent.
Propagation speed. Bounded by adoption rate. The speed at which harm accumulates is determined by how fast the AI
system is deployed, not by any interaction dynamic.
Intervention architecture. Agent-level capability evaluation. Existing single-agent safety frameworks (EU AI Act risk
categories, model evaluations, use-case restrictions) are adequate.
Relevance to severity threshold. T0 incidents cross the international coordination threshold only through scale — the
same harm replicated across a large number of independent deployments in many jurisdictions simultaneously. The
propagation is not qualitatively different from any other technology risk that scales with adoption.
F.3.2
T1: Common-cause correlation
Propagation scaling. Correlated: an exogenous shock triggers simultaneous failure across the agent population sharing
the upstream dependency. The scaling is determined by the upstream dependency, i.e. the fraction of the deployed agent
population sharing the common source. Algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021) transforms the
89


failure distribution from independently distributed (T0: self-limiting) to positively correlated across the entire dependent
population (Bommasani et al., 2022).
Cascade mechanism. Common-cause: a single failure event propagates from the shared upstream source to all
dependent agents in one step. There is no inter-agent cascade; agents fail simultaneously because they share a
vulnerability, not because one agent’s failure triggers another’s.
Propagation speed. Instantaneous relative to the upstream event. Once the shared source fails, all dependent agents are
affected simultaneously. The detection challenge is not speed of propagation but identification of the shared dependency
structure before the failure occurs.
Intervention architecture. Upstream source governance: model diversity requirements, stress-testing against common-
mode failures, supply-chain transparency, infrastructure resilience standards. The CrowdStrike outage (2024), in which
a single update simultaneously disabled approximately 8.5 million Windows devices, illustrates the T1 propagation
profile.
Relevance to severity threshold. T1 incidents cross the international coordination threshold when the shared upstream
source is global. T1 is the most tractable topology category for governance because the intervention target is identifiable
(audit and diversify the upstream source), but it is empirically under-studied for AI-specific dependencies.
F.3.3
T2: Hierarchical orchestration
Propagation scaling. Superlinear: N coordinated agents produce capabilities exceeding N× single-agent capability.
The scaling is determined by orchestration efficiency.
Cascade mechanism. Command propagation: instructions flow top-down from orchestrator to sub-agents. Failure at
the orchestrator level propagates to all subordinate agents in O(depth) steps. Conversely, a compromised orchestrator
converts all subordinate agents into vectors for the compromised objective.
Propagation speed. Determined by orchestration latency — typically seconds to minutes in current agentic AI
frameworks.
T2 as orthogonal dimension. T2 is structurally orthogonal to the T1–T3 spectrum. An orchestrated system can exhibit
T1 properties (sub-agents sharing common training data), T3 properties (sub-agents developing emergent coordination
beyond the orchestrator’s design), or both.
Intervention architecture. Orchestrator capability governance, usage monitoring for multi-provider API patterns,
coordination signature detection, and inbuilt operational guardrails.
Relevance to severity threshold. T2 incidents cross the international coordination threshold when orchestration spans
jurisdictions, when multi-provider model combinations evade single-provider safety measures, or when agentic systems
operate with cross-border scope. The Russian state-sponsored disinformation ecosystem documented in AIID Incidents
727, 884, 929, and 968 illustrates T2 orchestration with T3 emergence: a hierarchical command structure (GRU)
directed multiple AI-enabled operations across jurisdictions, while the downstream information environment exhibited
emergent dynamics beyond the orchestrator’s direct control. T2 is the fastest-growing real-world risk category.
F.3.4
T3: Emergent interaction
Propagation scaling. Emergent: the relationship between agent count and system-level outcome is non-linear,
potentially discontinuous, and not derivable from the properties of individual agents. Phase transitions (sudden,
non-linear, system-wide behavioral responses to small perturbations in inputs) are possible (Watts, 2002).
Cascade mechanism. Endogenous: small perturbations are amplified through feedback loops in the interaction structure.
Each agent’s response to the perturbed environment alters the environment further, creating a self-reinforcing cascade.
The cascade is a property of the interaction dynamics, not of any individual agent. Removing or replacing individual
agents does not interrupt the cascade if the interaction structure is preserved; the dynamics have been systemically
endogenized. In scale-free networks, single-contact transmission faces no effective epidemic threshold (Pastor-Satorras
and Vespignani, 2001); in networks with threshold-based activation, cascades occur only within a specific connectivity
window (Watts, 2002).
Propagation speed. Determined by interaction rate in the deployment environment. The same T3 dynamics propagate
in microseconds through high-frequency trading infrastructure (Kirilenko et al., 2017), in hours through social-media
recommendation systems, and in months through policy-advisory ecosystems. Propagation speed is an environmental
property.
90


Event morphing. T3 is the topology category where the character of an incident can change qualitatively as it
propagates. A biased hiring algorithm deployed in isolation produces biased decisions (T0). The same algorithm as one
of several sharing candidates and data produces correlated discrimination across a labor market (T1). If algorithms
begin conditioning on each other’s outputs, e.g. using competitor acceptance rates as signals, the system locks into
discriminatory equilibria persisting after the original bias is corrected (T3). The topology category escalates because
the interaction environment transformed how the underlying failure propagated.
Intervention architecture. Environmental restructuring: changing the payoff structure, information rules, or coupling
topology that enabled the harmful equilibrium. Agent-level intervention is insufficient. Circuit-breaker mechanisms —
automated interruption of interaction dynamics when measured coupling exceeds thresholds — are the most immediately
implementable governance innovation, by analogy with financial-market trading halts (Kirilenko et al., 2017).
Relevance to severity threshold. T3 is the topology category where existing governance frameworks are least adequate
and the case for international coordination is most acute. The interaction dynamics may span jurisdictions, no single
authority can observe the full interaction space, and the harm is a property of the interaction rather than of any
identifiable actor (Hammond et al., 2025; Helbing, 2013). Algorithmic pricing in fuel markets (Hammond et al., 2025)
illustrates the governance challenge: supra-competitive pricing can emerge from the interaction of independently
deployed algorithms conditioning on the same market signals, without any explicit agreement between operators or
malicious actor. Consumer harm comes about through the interactions between providers, and no single competition
authority can straightforwardly attribute the cause to an actor or remedy it.
F.4
Environmental structure as a determinant of propagation dynamics
A key element here is that the deployment environment is a constitutive component of the hazard: a model that passes
every single-agent safety evaluation can produce catastrophic outcomes when deployed into an environment whose
structure supports harmful equilibria (Perrow, 1999; Maas, 2018). We identify five important environmental dimensions
that shape the propagation profile.
F.4.1
Information structure
The observability regime of the deployment environment: public versus private signals, observability of other agents’
actions, and observability by oversight systems. The critical configuration for propagation risk is high inter-agent
observability combined with low regulatory observability. These are environments where all participants observe
the same signals but regulators cannot observe the participants’ responses. Monitoring infrastructure must close this
observability gap.
F.4.2
Payoff structure
The consequence architecture: zero-sum, positive-sum, or mixed-sum interactions; continuous versus binary outcome
spaces; reversible versus irreversible actions. Binary, irreversible payoff structures convert gradual risk accumulation
into sudden, catastrophic outcomes. The Cold War MAD equilibrium illustrates the extreme: different capabilities and
knowledge converged on the same strategic equilibrium because the payoff structure dominated the heterogeneity of the
agents involved. Environments with binary, irreversible payoffs should receive higher standing hazard ratings regardless
of detected anomalies.
F.4.3
Coupling structure
The network topology of agent interactions: hub-and-spoke versus distributed; direct agent-to-agent versus environment-
mediated interaction. Hub-and-spoke networks enable single-hop system-wide propagation. Distributed networks
propagate more slowly but are harder to contain. When tight couplings are present, perturbations propagate faster than
operators can respond, and this is Perrow’s precondition for normal accidents (Perrow, 1999). Interdependent networks
undergo abrupt cascading collapse where isolated networks degrade gradually (Buldyrev et al., 2010), and connections
that normally diversify risk become contagion channels under stress (Gai and Kapadia, 2010; Acemoglu et al., 2015).
F.4.4
Temporal structure
The interaction timescale: one-shot versus repeated interaction, the ‘shadow of the future’, and commitment mechanisms.
Temporal structure determines propagation speed directly, as the same underlying failure propagates at the rate set by
the environment’s interaction cycle. Detection-latency requirements follow: the monitoring system must operate faster
than the propagation dynamics it aims to detect. Environments with fast interaction cycles (high-frequency trading:
91


milliseconds) require automated, continuous monitoring; environments with slow cycles (policy advisory: months)
permit human-in-the-loop approaches.
F.4.5
Regulatory structure
Jurisdiction and scope of applicable governance. When the interaction scope of the AI + environment system exceeds
the observation scope of any single regulator, propagation can cross jurisdictional boundaries undetected. This is a
primary generator of the international coordination threshold: governance gaps emerge by construction when interaction
dynamics are global but regulatory observation is national (Helbing, 2013).
F.5
The T1→T3 transition: signal endogenization
The transition from T1 (common-cause correlation) to T3 (emergent interaction) is the most consequential propagation-
regime change for severity-threshold design, because it marks the point at which the governance approach must shift
from upstream-source control to interaction-structure intervention. The transition passes through three stages:
F.5.1
Stage 1: Sunspot correlation (near-T1)
Agents observe a common exogenous signal (a price feed, a data release, a shared training distribution) and they all
respond to it similarly because of shared architecture or training. Their behavior is correlated, but the correlation is
entirely attributable to the common signal. Removing the signal eliminates the correlation. The propagation structure is
a star graph: common signal →correlated responses, with no inter-agent edges.
Detection signature. High correlating information (mutual information) between agent outputs. Low or zero causal
information (transfer entropy) between agent outputs. Information flow is from signal to agents, not between agents.
F.5.2
Stage 2: Cheap talk (transition zone)
Agents begin to condition on each other’s observable behavior as well as on the exogenous signal. The exogenous
signal still drives the bulk of the correlation, but inter-agent observation introduces weak directed influence. Agents
may use language, pricing signals, or other observable outputs as de facto communication channels, transmitting
information about intentions or strategies without explicit coordination. Crandall et al. (2018) demonstrated this
mechanism experimentally: their S# algorithm uses costless signals, cheap talk, that acquire meaning through repeated
interaction, enabling cooperation rates rivalling human–human coordination in repeated 2 × 2 games. The signals are
formally payoff-irrelevant but become behaviorally relevant because agents learn to condition on them, bootstrapping
trust and mutual expectations through interaction history. This propagation structure adds inter-agent edges to the star
graph, creating a hybrid topology.
Detection signature. Correlating information remains high. Causal information between agent outputs begins to rise.
The ratio of causal to correlating information is the key diagnostic: a rising ratio signals that endogenous coupling is
developing within an environment that still appears to be driven by common-cause correlation.
F.5.3
Stage 3: Implicit coordination (T3)
Agents’ behavior is primarily determined by interaction dynamics rather than by the exogenous signal. The equilibrium
is self-sustaining: removing the original common signal does not break the coordination. The propagation structure is a
dense, feedback-rich graph with no necessary connection to the original exogenous signal.
Detection signature. Causal information between agent outputs is elevated and stable. The critical diagnostic is that
causal information remains elevated even when the original common signal is perturbed or removed, indicating an
endogenized coupling between agents.
Empirical anchors. The Calvano et al. (2020) algorithmic-collusion result is the cleanest empirical T3 case: Q-learning
pricing agents discover supra-competitive pricing through endogenous market signals alone, with no communication
channel, no shared upstream cause, and no orchestrator. The progression from Q-learning (Calvano et al., 2020) through
LLM market division (Lin et al., 2024) to steganographic channels (Motwani et al., 2024) illustrates the evolution of
risks: implicit coordination →cheap talk via language →covert signalling channels that increasingly resist oversight.

F.6
Information-theoretic measurement signatures
The detection of topology categories and transitions between them requires measurement infrastructure that can distin-
guish correlation from causation in agent-interaction data. The core measurement framework uses two complementary
quantities:
Correlating information (operationalized as mutual information or computationally tractable proxies such as Theil
decomposition indices; Theil, 1989; Harré, 2022) captures the degree of statistical association between agent outputs. It
detects synchronisation between agents’ behaviors but cannot determine whether the similarity arises from common
cause (T1) or mutual influence (T3).
Causal information (operationalized as transfer entropy or Granger-causal measures; Barnett et al., 2009; Harré,
2022) captures directed, time-asymmetric information flow between agent outputs. It detects one agent’s behavior
systematically predicting changes in another’s (i.e. causal influence) and can distinguish T1 (no inter-agent causal flow)
from T3 (elevated inter-agent causal flow).

Early-warning signals. The detection of approaching tipping points by non-stationary statistical measures is well

correlating information peaks at the transition as system-wide synchronisation takes hold. Different measures detect
