measurement system.
Persistent gap. Across all fields where early-warning detection has been developed, the detection of approaching
transitions is typically not connected to the cost of the transition in domain-relevant terms. Early-warning signals can
indicate a market crash is approaching, but not whether the crash will destroy 5% or 40% of capital. Closing this gap
by linking statistical detection to quantified impact estimation is the central methodological challenge for monitoring
multi-agent AI incidents.
F.7
Operationalisation as escalation triggers
F.7.1
Value-at-Risk analogy
One approach to operationalizing the measurement signatures is analogous to Value-at-Risk (VaR) methods in finance:
characterize the distribution of information-measure fluctuations during quiescent periods and use percentile bounds
(e.g. 95th or 99th percentile) as calibrated risk thresholds. An exceedance of the 99th percentile for causal information
between agents in a previously T1-classified system would constitute a statistical trigger indicating a possible T1→T3
transition.
93


Calibrating the relationship between a percentile exceedance and the expected magnitude of real-world impact is
domain-specific and requires both simulation and accumulating empirical data, but the framework provides a principled
basis for connecting statistical detection to the threshold logic developed in the main text.
F.7.2
Topology-sensitive escalation
The cost of late detection varies by topology category and environmental structure:
T0. Conventional risks. Detection latency is bounded by adoption speed. Existing single-agent frameworks are
adequate.
T1 and early T1→T3 transition. Early detection can enable effective intervention through circuit breakers, diversity
requirements, or interaction-protocol constraints. The intervention window exists because the coupling is not yet
self-sustaining.
Established T3. Intervention options narrow considerably. The equilibrium is endogenous and self-sustaining;
disrupting it requires restructuring the interaction environment itself, for example changing the payoff structure, the
information rules, or the coupling topology. Agent-level remediation is insufficient.
Environmental modulation. The same detected anomaly warrants faster escalation in a tightly coupled environment
than in a loosely coupled one. In a tightly coupled, fast-interaction environment (high-frequency trading), late detection
of T3 dynamics may mean the harmful equilibrium is already locked in before any governance response is possible. In
a loosely coupled, slow-interaction environment (policy-advisory systems), the same T3 dynamics develop over months,
giving governance systems time to intervene.
F.7.3
Standing hazard assessment
Beyond the detection of anomalies in ongoing dynamics, the environmental structure itself should be assessed as a
standing hazard indicator. Even in the absence of detected anomalies, environments with the following structural
properties have inherently higher propagation potential for multi-agent AI incidents:
• Tight coupling (perturbations propagate faster than operators can respond)
• Fast interaction cycles (milliseconds to hours rather than days to months)
• Binary, irreversible payoff structures (elections, military engagements, critical infrastructure)
• Jurisdictional gaps (interaction scope exceeds any single regulator’s observation scope)
• High inter-agent observability with low regulatory observability
This prospective assessment, whereby environments are flagged where the structure is conducive to dangerous propa-
gation profiles, complements the retrospective detection of anomalies and can be conducted before any AI system is
deployed into the environment.
F.7.4
Integration with existing regulatory monitoring
Where historical data exist through conventional regulatory processes — such as financial regulators tracking volatility,
correlation structures, and order flow; energy regulators monitoring grid stability and frequency deviations; and
competition authorities tracking pricing patterns and market concentration — these macro-state variables constitute an
existing observational infrastructure against which AI-mediated changes can be benchmarked.
This macro-state monitoring provides a first-pass detection layer: low-specificity indicators that warrant targeted
investigation using the information-theoretic measures described above, or other more targeted investigations where
appropriate. An effective AI-incident monitoring framework does not need to build all observational infrastructure from
scratch; it can integrate with existing regulatory monitoring, using changes in already tracked macro-variables as the
initial anomaly signal, especially where dense historical data already exist as a baseline.
The fundamental constraint is that current detection is late. Interaction-emergent failures are typically identified after
the fact — through market anomalies, security incidents, media reports, or user complaints — rather than through
real-time monitoring. Continuous, system-level measurement infrastructure operating across providers, jurisdictions,
and deployment contexts is a prerequisite for any escalation framework that aims to be preventive rather than reactive.

Abstract: AI incident reporting requirements are emerging in regulation and policy, yet no operational criteria exist for determining when a detected AI incident warrants escalation beyond national handling to international coordination. This paper proposes an escalation framework to address this gap, intended as a common reference point across jurisdictions that enables aligned escalation while preserving flexibility in how actors respond within their own legal and policy contexts. Our methodology involves a review of SB 53, the EU AI Act, the GPAI Code of Practice, and incident frameworks from other industries, to derive eight criteria to assess whether an incident warrants escalation, which we then translate into a sequential flowchart with gated decision points and threshold checks. For each criterion, we map how it interplays with the EU AI Act, SB 53, and the GPAI Code of Practice, identifying where these frameworks’ design choices support or undermine effective detection. We test the framework against ten documented AI incidents and structured variants to identify where escalation criteria under-detect or misclassify incidents in practice. We find three design patterns that may lead to systematic under-detection or misclassification of AI incidents in regimes where model developers are responsible for escalation: (a) where escalation requires confirmed harm, events such as model weight exfiltration or credible CBRN threats risk detection only after severe, irreversible harm has propagated, as developers who observe the risk materializing cannot confirm downstream harms; (b) where incidents are assessed only individually, systemic harms emerging from accumulation — such as large-scale manipulation and psychological harm — risk being under-detected; and (c) where thresholds align with legal instruments rather than quantitatively testable terms, criteria risk being impractical to apply under time pressure.
